speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. SPEAKER REEFERS TO LANGUAGE USED BY MR. GAUTHIER.
speechtext:
My attention has been directed to language used during the debate last evening by the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe at a time when I happened to be out of the Chamber. The hon. member (Mr. Gauthier) is reported in Hansard to have said:
His amendment (Mr. Barrette's), being a negative one, would have been ruled out of order if it had not been introduced with the consent of the Government.
It seems to me that the implication contained in these words is unmistakable, and one which if allowed to go unchallenged would seriously impair my usefulness as Speaker of this House. I need hardly say that the use of such language by an hon. member of the House is not in conformity with the usual practice in such cases, and is not in keeping with the spirit of proper decorum in debate. When the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe is in his place I purpose to ask him to withdraw this language.

subtopic: NUMBER OF JURORS IN PANEL.

speechtext: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 97, to amend the criminal code.

subtopic: NUMBER OF JURORS IN PANEL.
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: NUMBER OF JURORS IN PANEL.
speechtext:
Our attention has been called to the fact that by recent legislation in the province of Manitoba, as well as by legislation which has been in force for some

time in some of the other provinces, there is no fixed number of jurors to be summoned as constituting the panel, power being given to the judge to summon any number of jurors that he may deem desirable for the purposes of the business to be brought before the court. Under this legislation the panel may be of a very large number, and the Crown in any trial has the right to stand aside any number of jurors as they are called, without assigning any reason. Wherever under the law the panel is fixed at a definite number, this right of stand aside is of course limited to the number fixed for the panel, and, the panel once exhausted, these jurors may be called again and, unless there is ground for challenge, will be entitled to sit. It was considered not desirable that the Crown should have this right to stand aside extending to such an indefinite number, or rather, that it should not have that right without its being subject to the same control which is confided to the judge as to the determination of the number of the panel. This Bill therefore proposes to amend that section of the Criminal Code by limiting the right of stand aside to the number of forty-eight, which is the fixed number of the panel in many of the provinces, was such in Manitoba, until the recent legislation, unless the judge for special cause permits the right to be exercised as regards a larger number. In other words, the purpose is simply to subject the right of stand aside to the same control on the pari of the judge as under the provincial legislation referred to he has over the number of the panel.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 98, to amend the Exchequer Court Act.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This Bill contains two clauses. The purpose of the first is to make provision for the liability for costs on the part of litigants with the Crown where the case on the part of the Crown is conducted by the department. In those cases the lawyers in the department are not entitled to collect fees or costs for themselves, they being paid by their salaries. It is thought desirable, notwithstanding that fact, that litigants who bring unfounded claims

against the Grown should be liable for costs the same as any other litigant. The purpose of this first clause is therefore to provide that in such cases the costs to which the litigants may be condemned shall be payable to the Crown simply, the Crown paying its own costs through the salaries of its officers.
The other provision of the Bill is to achieve a purpose which was also the purpose of a Bill introduced earlier in. the session by the hon. member for Kamour-aska (Mr. Lapointe), if my memory serves me right. The matter dealt with by that proposed Bill of his had already been brought to our attention before his Bill was introduced, and we had come to the conclusion that an amendment such as he sought to make by his Bill should be made to the Exchequer Court Act. The clause of the Exchequer Court Act sought to be amended by this Bill and by the Bill of the hon. member for Kamouraska is the clause giving jurisdiction to the court to adjudicate upon any claim of damages against the Crown resulting from death or injury to person or property caused by the negligence of any servant of the Crown upon a public work. The Supreme Court has interpreted the section as it now stands as limiting the liability to cases where the injury is actually sustained upon the public work; that is to say, where the person suffering is actually on the public work or where it is a question of damage to property which property itself is actually upon the public work. This created a situation in which, though a man might be injured by the negligence of an employee of the Crown in the course of his employment, and where the whole cause of the injury took place upon the public work, yet if the victim himself was not actually on the public work he had no recourse.
While there is no reason to criticise the interpretation put by the Supreme Court upon the section as it stands, I do not think it was intended when the legislation was originally enacted to make that distinction, namely, to make the liability depend upon the locality .in which the individual or the property injured happened to be.
The purpose of this legislation is simply so to amend the section that the Crown will be liable-as I certainly believe was intended-for damage or injury resulting from the negligence of an employee of the Crown within the scope of his employment upon a public work. It simply does away with the requirement which the present sec-

tion has been interpreted as containing, namely, that the individual or property injured should at the moment be actually on the public work.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 99, to amend the Interest Act.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The purpose of this
Bill is to make the raite of interest payable upon judgments in the province of Manitoba similar to that payable in the province of Alberta and Saskatchewan, and I think in almost tall the other provinces. The necessity for this legislation arises because of the fact that it has recently been decided that the interest upon judgments in the province of Manitoba runs 'at but 4 per cent, which I understand was the rate fixed by English statute at the time the English lafr became applicable to the province of Manitoba.
The courts appear to have held that it was not within the jurisdiction of a provincial legislature to legislate on the subject of interest, even interest running upon a judgment, and that consequently any modification of the law in that regard attempted by the provincial legislature was ineffective. From many sources in Manitoba have come requests that the interest rate there should be made the same as that ^ provided for by statute for the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, which is the ordinary rate of interest, five per cent provided in cases where neither by law nor by agreement is the rate of interest fixed. There have been requests from Manitoba also that the interest rate should be made higher than this. While it did not appear to us that there should be a higher rate of interest in Manitoba than in other provinces, it did appear desirable that there should be an equal rate. This Bill, therefore, simply brings the province of Manitoba under the provisions made applicable to the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, under which interest runs upon a judgment at the rate of five per cent.
What is the rate of interest, under such circumstances, in Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My impression is that it is five per cent. I know that it is five
per cent in the province of Quebec. I think that in one or more of the Maritime Provinces it is six per cent.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.

maintopic: SPEECH OF MR. L. J. GAUTHIER.
subtopic: THE PRIME MINISTER DENIES STATEMENTS MADE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my attention has been directed just now to a statement made yesterday by the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe (Mr. L. J. Gauthier), to which Your Honour has alluded. I observe, also, in the speech of the hon. member another statement of somewhat the same character. The first statement to which I wish to allude is this:
We are engaged in a very serious debate, but permit me to say that I consider this amendment to the amendment to be a farce. It has been engineered, not by the mover and seconder of the motion, but by the Government itself.
Further on he says, referring to the same amendment proposed by the hon. member for Berthier:
His amendment, being a negative one, would have been ruled out of order if it had not been introduced with the consent of the Government.	,
I desire to give these statements the most unqualified denial. I neither heard, nor knew anything of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Berthier until I saw it the following morning in the newspapers. Any intention to propose such an amendment was never communicated to me; nor, in so far as I am aware, to any of my colleagues. The Government, from first to last, had absolutely nothing to do with the proposed amendment, and we will oppose it in the most unqualified manner.

Mr. BARRETTE (Berthier), (translation): Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege I found in Hansard, this morning that the honourable member for St. Hyacinthe (Mr. Gauthier) had stated yesterday before this House that the Government had inspired the amendment to the amendment which I did propose to the conscription Bill.
I emphatically deny the honourable Prime Minister or any of his colleagues or followers having had anything to do either director Wilfrid Laurier.]
ly or indirectly with this amendment to the amendment. I am even ready to resign my seat in this House to prove my statement.
I make this denial, not because I am in the least afraid of what may be stated by my honourable friend from St. Hyacinthe, whose speech has stirred up general indignation throughout the country, but because I wish to set the facts in their proper light. speechtext:
-Consideration of the motion ,of the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden (Prime Minister) for the second reading of Bill No. 75, Military Service Act, 1917, and the amendment of Sir Wilfrid Laurier thereto, and on the amendment t.o the amendment by Mr. Barrette, resumed from Thursday, June 21.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (South Renfrew) :	Mr. Speaker, as a great portion of
my public life has -been devoted to defending the rights of minorities, even to the point of generosity, as charged by my opponents, to-day, being in the minority arriong my own friends, I ask from them the kind consideration which I h-ave always endeavoured to extend to them. We are asking the men of Canada to be : Ready, aye ready. We, in this House, -might add a slogan for our own benefit: Be steady, aye

steady. If there ever was a time in the history of this country when men should curb their passions and prejudices simultaneously with their tongues, that time is now, and this is the place. Nothing can he gained, Mr. Speaker, by recrimination. We are citizens of a common country, having the same ideal, having the same object, and, I take it, every man in this House no matter from what province he may come, or from w'hat stock he may have sprung, believes in his country, is attached to his country, and believes, further, that the destiny of his country is bound up in its relationship with the great British Empire. We may differ on details, but only on details. Sir, the people of Canada, the people of the Empire, and the nations of the earth, are looking at Canada .at the present moment. Should we say or do aught to disturb the harmony that exists among the people of different origin in this country, we will add to the gratification of our enemies and detract from the comfort of our friends.
In attempting to speak as one of the minority on this side of the House, I do it without any trepidation. I say, frankly, if I were on the other side of the House,
I would not feel such freedom. Liberalism, as I have learned it, allows the fullest freedom of thought to every member who advocates Liberalism, and I want to say that, while I differ with my revered leader, I have his absolute consent to take whatever course I think best at the present time. Every member on this side of the House is at liberty to act, speak, and vote as he chooses, and, by. doing so, he is not severing the ties of affection that bind him to his grand old chieftain, neither is he slinking aw.ay, in any sense, from the great Liberal party and the causes which it has always stood for. We have had, Sir, attacks made on my revered leader. I resent those attacks just as warmly today as I would, or could, if he and I were agreeing. We are not disagreeing on any essential a bit more than members of different churches are disagreeing on the one essential belief, and trying to get to heaven, each picking his own path. The great Liberal chieftain stands to-day where he has always stood, as the advocate of what he thinks is best for Canada and for the Empire. He is as anxious about winning -this great struggle as I am. He sees difficulties in the way, in my point of view, but he recognizes my right to have that viewpoint. I do not see those difficulties, but I want to point out 
that he and I, as well as every member of this House, are joined in one resolve that our best must be done for the winning of this great struggle, and it is only on the details of how that is to be accomplished that I differ from him. I may be wrong in my attitude, and he may be right. Young men might forget that, when they were boys, the Liberal chieftain was fighting for the great principles, the benefits of which they now enjoy. In 1896, facing the greatest opposition, and the greatest influence that was ever brought to bear on man in this country, he stood for the principle of provincial rights, and other men from the province of Quebec stood behind him on that principle, and, as >a result, it was established. He was right. Those who sat on the other side of the House were wrong. That may be the case in this instance. On the question of the Canadian, navy, the events of this moment prove that my leader was right

speechtext:
I would ask hon. gentlemen who live in the interior of Canada to go to the Pacific and to the Atlantic coasts, and come back and tell us what they find that they would not have found, if there had been a Canadian navy. In 1911 my leader was again right, as the Government has acknowledged by its action. He may be right in this case, but I think he is not. We differ, having both one object in view.
Sir, just a word or two as to our fellow citizens from the province of Quebec. We cannot get anywhere in this country by recrimination. Readers of Canadian history must not forget-they cannot forget, though some gentlemen speak as if they were not conversant with Canadian history -that the fact that to-day we are still a portion of the British Empire is due in a measure to the loyalty of the Frenchmen, of the province of Quebec in the years gone by. During recent years, in the province of Quebec, our fellow citizens have not been imbued with the military spirit with which we in the other provinces are imbued. They have not in Quebec, throughout the villages and small towns, the drill halls and military centres to the extent that we have them in Ontario.^ They have not had a centre of military education, by having officers stationed all through the province of Quebec. They have gone their way, as we have gone ours in the other provinces, believing that the time would not come, for

many, many years at least, when they would be called on to perform military service. We must meet the situations as we find them, and we cannot possibly by vituperative language, accomplish the purpose we have in view.
Having said this, I want to refer to another matter. The French race is much more logical than we>are. There are very few English-speaking members of this House who know the French Canadian character as intimately as I do; I have had daily business relations with the French Canadian people. They are brave, chivalrous, truthful; above all, they are logical. Having been told time and again by the leader of the Government and the leader of the Opposition that there would be no conscription in Canada, they hardly bdlieve it possible that conscription has been proposed. They cannot understand it. They are logical, but we are not. We can change with conditions much more readily than can our French Canadian fellow-citizens. These considerations must be borne in mind. in the discussion of the question now before the House. It is the duty of those who differ from the French Canadian people to look at these matters from their viewpoint and to discuss them accordingly. To my mind, the surest way of 'being fair is to put ourselves in the other man's position, to find out what we should do if we were subject to his environment, his history, his characteristics. If every one does that there will be an exemplification of what is best; there will be not recrimination, but a closer drawing together of the two races, with the result that after this Bill is passed it may not be necessary to put it into operation.
There are three classes of Canadians: those who have gone to the front, those who cannot go, and those who ought to go. Of those who have gone nothing too good can be said. They have gone from Quebec and from Ontario, from the East and from the West, from the families of the rich, of the middle classes, and of the poor. Mingling on the field of battle, irrespective of the position that they held in this country in the way of class or occupation, they are fighting side by side in order that, your children and mine may enjoy tha{, liberty and freedom of individual action which has always been the pride of our race. In that respect there is no distinction of class. I know men of great wealth who have sent practically all their sons, some of whom have suffered; all honour to these sons and to these parents. I know the sons of work-
164 i
men who have gone. Many widows have sent their only sons, some of whom have died, leaving the mothers without support and without comfort. The people of Canada are imbued with the spirit of sacrifice, knowing full well that if we lose in this great struggle nothing is left to us who so long have prized the liberties which we enjoy. Our forefathers fought in 1812; better a thousand times that we had lost in 1812 than that we should lose in 1917. Had we lost in 1812 to-day we should be under another form of democratic government-that would be the only change. But if we lose in this conflict we lose all that democratic government stands for; we become not our own masters, but tfie slaves of others.
This brings me to the matter of recruiting. I do not wish to indulge in undue criticism, but having taken part in the work of recruiting, so far as I could in my own feeble way, I think I am in a position to point to some of the reasons why the voluntary system failed. When the war broke out, recruiting leagues, designated by various names, but all working for a common purpose, were formed throughout Ontario. But from the Government's standpoint there was no organization. Any man in this House from the province of Ontario who will recall the recruiting operations in his own territory will realize that the successful work along this line was done by civilian organizations. Not only did these civilians work, but they paid the expenses as well; there is, I suppose, not a man in this House who has not paid out large sums of money from his own pocket in order to assist the work of recruiting in Ms own vicinity. If we had had proper Government organization in Ontario-I speak of that province only

recruiting would have been 25 per cent greater than it was. To the citizens of that province, much more than to the Government, is due the credit for the success of recruiting in Ontario.

speechtext: Why should not the same course have been followed in Quebec?

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING AND ON THE AMENDMENTS.
speechtext:
I shall come to Quebec in a moment; my hon. friend must not worry. If I leave anything out, and the House, having not wearied of my remarks, will direct my attention to it, I shall deal with it.
This, then, is my first criticism of the Government: there was no real organization in the matter of recruiting. It is true that recruiting officers were sent here and there. I look into the faces of men who

spoke at various meetings and who had charge of various committees. They will agree with me that many of the recruiting officers were of no value whatever to them in getting recruits. I do not wish to speajc disparagingly of those officers, but they were not the right men to get recruits. Some officers were sent out who hindered civilians from getting recruits. I have stood on the platform with men for whose language I* had to apologize in order to bring the audience back to a frame of mind in which they would consider my request [DOT]for recruits. No man can hope for success in recruiting who begins by abusing the young men or the older men and calling them slackers. Tkat is not the way *to get recruits. We had too much of that in Ontario, and our recruiting was not what it should have been.
The first real jolt that was given by the Government to recruiting in Ontario was when the ex-Minister of Militia said that he was getting more men than he needed. At the first meeting that I attended after that statement had been made, I was laughed at. Men said: we understand that the Government are having no trouble in getting men; that they are getting more men than they can equip; that the men are climbing over each other to enlist. For months that statement of the then Minister of. Militia was a serious handicap, because the men naturally concluded that if the Government were getting more men than they could equip, there was no use in enlisting until the work was caught up. This emphasizes my contention that there was lack of organization, somewhere, somehow.
Then other things came up; I do not want to refer to them in a critical way. The, manufacturer was not allowed to sell [DOT]directly to the department; people got in 'between, and were receiving certain com-*missions. This tended to greatly injure Tecruiting in Ontario. The ex-Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes) told us the other day that the Prime Minister himself, after Sir Thomas, now Baron, Shaughnessy issued a certain statement, intimated that the pressure upon recruiting might be relieved for a little time. I think the exminister said that the Minister of Finance brought back that report after a visit to Toronto.

I come now to Quebec. Hon. gentlemen have referred to the appointment as chief recruiting officer of a clergyman of the church to which I belong. That may seem a small matter, but as I said in the beginning of my remarks, if we are to accomplish ,our object, which I presume is the securing of recruits, we must meet the people with whom we have to deal from their own viewpoint. We might as well expect the Archbishop of Montreal to be appointed editor of the Orange Sentinel, as to have a Methodist clergyman, np matter how great a preacher he is, chief recruiting officer amongst the French Canadian people. That, however, is only a minor matter.
1 come now to a more delicate point, and I raised this question in this House in the early_ stages of the war. I wish to speak of this without any recrimination, without even questioning for the moment the standpoint of the men to whom I refer, but merely as a matter of history and of fact. Since the war began, I said in this House that the doctrine preached previously to 1911 by certain people in Quebec, namely: that we owed nothing to Britain and should not send a man to fight her battles, had more to do with slowness of recruiting in Quebec than any other cause. Another cause was that when the war broke out the Government of Canada had as three of its members,, men who had taken 4 p.m. that position at every church door in Quebec, and the young men to whom this Government was appealing to enlist had been told by those men that it was no part of their duty to enlist to fight overseas. As I have said before, the French mind is logical; you cannot turn it upside down over night, and when men were found in the Government, helping to direct the affairs of this war, who .had told the young men of Quebec^ that such a war was no concern of theirs, those young men challenged the sincerity of the men who were asking them to enlist.^ Under similar circumstances any one in Ontario would have done the same thing; I certainly would have; I would not have listened, under like circumstances, to any appeal. Further than that, when this war broke out, the Government of Canada had not a French speaking member in it who cared to go on the platform in Quebec and ask for recruits.

I am not sure but that such is true, but it would not be an excuse here. They are building their own ships and working away. Although this condition was called to the attention of the Government as likely to arise, we find that the Government railway itself got so far behind with rolling stock that a few days after the new manager was appointed he ordered no less than 5,000 box cars and several engines.
Let me speak of the co-ordination of industry in natural resources. A great many of our industries have been taken charge of by the Imperial Munitions Board, find some of them have been pretty well organized, but there are still in Canada industries that are turning out goods which are not essential to the prosecution of the war. They are turning out goods that are luxuries, not essentials, not necessaries. There ought to be a sizing up of all these industries and every industry that is not producing something that can be used in the war, or which is a necessity, ought to be asked to turn its attention in some other direction in order that the war may he car. ried on more successfully. The industries of Canada have shown that they can pro' duce anything that can be produced anywhere in the world, as well and as cheaply. An inventory of the various industries of this country should be taken and those that are producing non-essential goods might well have their efforts directed to the production of necessary goods. Co-ordination of that kind would prevent overlapping between industries and we would have turned out in Canada in one steady stream from our own industries the things which are required for the prosecution of the war, and we would not find ourselves short of one commodity at a time when there was a big surplus of some other commodity.
Then, take our natural resources. The first thing this Government should have done was to have taken a firm grip of the nickel supply of the Dominion .of Canada.

That is one of the very essentials of modern warfare and modern shipbuilding, and by no circuitous r.oute, but by a direct grip of the hand, this Government should have taken possession of the nickel mines, or taken control, at least, and should have seen that the nickel products of Canada went for the benefit of the Allies, and for nobody else. And also that they went at the cheapest price, and if necessary, this Government should have had a nickel refinery industry in Canada, managed and worked by itself. Thus all the nickel should go straight to the Allies, and not through any other channel. We have our fishing industry, and we have been told, in the recent report, that fish is one of the best foods that could be sent to the Old Land, but, to a large extent, that export has fallen down. Why? Because arrangement has not been made with the railways to carry this freight by refrigerator cars, in which it could have been sent in greater quantities, than by express. The fishing industry has been neglected, and that industry, which should have supplied fish in great quantities, has practically fallen down, or largely so. I understand that a prominent gentleman who was here to propagate the fish industry in Canada for the benefit of our boys.at the front, has gone to the Old Land, to endeavour to form a company, and to come back here, and do what the Canadian Government should have done months ago. I will- now refer to our other minerals, coal, oil, gas, and I might say shale.

Now I come to a consideration of the proposal for a referendum. I claim to be a democrat; I believe in the people being consulted. But let me say to the House and to ^ the country that the Government are going to consult the people; they are getting ready for an election. Since the day the Minister of Public Works put his foot on the ship to go across the seas to visit the ^ soldiers, the Government have been getting ready for an election. The Prime Minister himself, in a suggestion made some days ago, intimated that the people ought to be consulted before this Bill is put into force. I took that as an indication that there was to be a general election. But we had another indication last-night. When an- hon. gentleman on this side was speaking^ about a referendum or an appeal to the people, the member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) asked him if he would be satisfied if the people were appealed to immediately through a general election. The member for St. Antoine is close to the Government; I took it for granted that he had been discussing the matter with the Government and was trying to find out what the members thought about the proposal of a general election.
I think, therefore, that there will be a general election, when tins question as well as others can be threshed out. Perhaps the best way to clear the atmosphere and to arrive at a -solution of the difficulties which present themselves is to go to the people and have them say what we are to do and who are to do it. I take no stock in the objection to a referendum because of its taking time; if anything, a referendum could be had in shorter time than a general election. But I believe that the people of Canada will be asked to divide on this issue among us as individuals

'for on this question we are not divided into parties; many gentlemen on the other side of the House accept the view of gentlemen on this side, and some on this side hold the view entertained by gentlemen opposite. We will have to go to our electors upon our personal attitude in this matter; and I am not sure, as I have said, but that an 
appeal to the people would -clear the atmosphere as nothing else would.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I trust that my remarks upon this momentous occasion will be, both in tone and in character, in accord with the moderation which has marked the speeches of most of those who have preceded me, and will be.in keeping with the importance of the measure now before the House and with the extreme gravity of the conditions which have brought it forth.
This is one of the greatest debates that have ever taken place in this House. Grea-t issues bring forth -great speeches, and great speeches are founded upon conviction. Hon. gentlemen on both sides of this House have during this debate spoken from full hearts the words of sincerity and truth. I think I can understand the wrench that it gives a man to sever the ties of his allegiance to a party with which he has been connected for many years. But we on this side of the House realize that hon. gentlemen opposite, and those on this side who differ from their leaders, are actuated by conviction, and, so far as we are concerned, there is no ignoble satisfaction at seeing hon. gentlemen opposite detach themselves, on an issue such as this, from the ranks of that party to which for so many years they have been connected. While, as I say, I shall emulate the moderation of most of those wfoo have spoken in this debate, I shall not follow the example of my hon. friend (Mr. Graham). He commenced by pointing out the futility of recrimination, and, possibly unconsciously to himself, because he is a politician who has for many years fought the battles of party, he indulged in not a little of that recrimination which he deprecated at the beginning of his remarks. He referred to the contest of 1911, and the action of Nationalist members upon the platform in Quebec. Is argument of that kind likely to advance the issue in this House? Should I add to the information of this House or gain any weight in the persuasiveness of my remarks if I harked back to an earlier date and quoted the leader of the Opposition upon many occasions on which he uttered sentiments to which he subscribed then, but to which he might or might not subscribe now, but which, I sub-

mit, would not be relevant to the consideration of this issue?
I purpose, therefore, confining myself to the question, namely, the Military Service Bill, which is now before the House. I shall touch lightly upon some of the matters referred to by my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) with regard to the organization and mobilization of the resources of this country; but it seems to me that those matters, while I admit they are somewhat, though remotely, relevant to this discussion, might be better dealt with on another and different occasion when some subject other than this Bill, which has evoked so much feeling, which is of so much importance, is before the House for consideration.
We are considering the necessity and the principle of compulsory military service in Canada. Hitherto the effort of Canada has been put forward under the voluntary system of enlistment. The effort which Canada has put forth under that system has been wonderful; it has been such as to command the admiration of the world, and I believe it will for all time stand to the credit, the renown, the honour and the glory of -Canada, that by voluntary effort she has been able to do what she has done. I do not regard the effort which Canada has put forth under the voluntary
5 p.m. system as having been a failure;
I say, on the contrary, that that effort was a magnificent success. Unfair and unjust it was, as enlistment under the voluntary system always is unjust and unfair, because the burden is cast upon the most patriotic in the community; but unsuccessful, it was not; it ~was a wonderful, success. My h,on. friend has criticised the Government for not organizing the country better in the carrying out of the voluntary system; he says that recruiting has been carried on principally by civilians. Does that detract in any way from the glory of the achievement? The Government takes the initiative in matters of this kind, and to the extent that it can secure the assistance and sympathy of citizens, to that extent will the effort the more succeed; and I desire to pay this tribute to the ex-Minister of Militia.
The energy which he put forth and the enthusiasm which be displayed at the outset of the war had much to do with the magnificent results accomplished by Canada under the voluntary enlistment system. It has been found in all States, n,o matter how patriotic they may be, that there comes a time, if they are engaged in a life and
death struggle, when the voluntary system fails, and when the State must, by compulsory service, enlist the manhood of the country if the State is to be saved. That happened in England, the Mother Country of individual and constitutional freedom? The voluntary system broke down there, and in order that the nation might be saved, resort was had to the compulsory system. Great-hearted Abraham Lincoln, as my right hon. friend who is a great admirer of his character knows, had to resort to the draft in order that the Union might be saved in the War of Secession, and to-day the United States, the greatest of the republican communities of the world, after having the benefit of the experience of other nations during the past three years, has resorted to the selective draft, and no less than 10,000,000 of her sons have come forward and enrolled. That is the position.
Canada's effort under the voluntary enlistment plan was a wonderful success, but voluntary enlistment has run its course, and we are now considering a system of compulsory military service which will organize and mobilize selectively the manhood of this country in order that we may continue to play our part in the prosecution of this -war. The fact is that the world and its civilization cannpt be saved, in this great crisis, by the voluntary system as against Germany organized under the Prussian military system. Compulsory military service has been adopted in France, the United States, Great Britain, and New Zealand, and I believe it will in time be adopted in Australia. We have reached the stage in Canada to-day when, if we are to continue to play our part in this war, if we are to continue tp take our share in the national defence, and above all, if we are to observe our obligations of honour to the men who have gone and whp represent us at the front, we must resort to compulsory military service; we must adopt this Bill.
This war is not like other wars in history. In the vastness of its scale, in its issues the most vital to humanity, in its menace the most dread to civilization, this war is different from all other wars, and so far as we can judge it is not near its conclusion. We have not even reached the crisis of this war. Three years of war behind us! How many years of war before us? The situation is of the gravest kind and the question before us is: Shall Canada's efforts slacken; .shall we continue to put forth our utmost strength, or shall we quit? From men of the blood of both races in

this House I think there can only be one answer. Canada must continue to put forth the utmost of her effort. And for how long? Until this war is determined in our favour, until the Hohenzollerns are utterly vam-quished. It is more than a war of nations, it is a war of conflicting ideals, and it will go on until one set of ideals is firmly established and the other utterly uprooted and overthrown. There can be no truce, there can be no peace, until the issue is victory for the Allies, and for Canada as one of the Allies. The war must go on; I think that is common ground for both sides of the House.
Let us not think this war is nearly won. Opposed to us is the greatest foe that ever confronted humanity, Germany, with her
70.000.	000 of people; Austria with 50,000,000, Turkey with 30,000,000, occupying together a compact territory with interior lines of communication. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister said upon his return from Great Britain that the Central Empires had
1.000.	000 more men in the field this spring
than they had last spring. Their line still extends from the North Sea to the confines of Switzerland; there is still a line of a thousand miles between the Central Empires and Russia. We read of great battles in which tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of men fall; we gain a mile or two miles or three miles, but the fact remains that the line on the Western front and the line on the Eastern front are substantially where they were a year ago. I say substantially, but I am the first to say that great progress has been made considering the conditions of modern warfare, for modern warfare is a warfare of attrition. It is a wearing:down process; the killing of more men on one side than on the other; the breaking down of morale and the exhausting of resources; that is modern warfare. But we have still before us the greatest enemy that ever confronted mankind, organized in every department of its national life, grim, determined that no effort shall be spared, that all power shall be put forth in order that they may impose their will upon humanity, that they may Germanize the world. There is as much need, nay, there is more need for .great effort to-day than there was at the outset, or at any time since the war began. From that German menace no nation, I care not how remote it may be, is free. The smallest nation or colony separated from Europe by thousands of leagues of sea is subject to the menace of German agression.	.

It has been put forward in this House that Canada is in no danger of an invasion. If that is so, to what is it due? Is it not due to the British fleet and to those men of French and British 'blood, who, month in and month out, have withstood the hosts of Germany in France and Flanders? Is it not due to the Canadians and New Zealanders and the others of our Allies who have met the enemy in the gates? If there is no danger of invasion, if there has been no such danger to Canada, it is only because we have been protected by the British fleet and by our Allies and our own heroes who have withstood the Hun on the battlefields of Europe.
Let me ask another question, and I am discussing this phase of the matter because it has been put forward that Canada should not send her forces outside this country unless to repel apprehended invasion. Supposing the Germans had taken Paris in their first rush, as they intended; supposing the British fleet had been defeated-if one can imagine such a thing-and that the Germans had reached London. Supposing they had been in a position to compel capitulation on the part of France and Great Britain. What would have happened to this country? Without landing a man upon these shores, the enemy could have compelled the cession of Canada. I say that it is within the plans of the German autocracy, within the world plans of German militarism, if not now, at a later date, to break up the British Empire and enter into and possess it. All their actions for years past have been in accordance with that view. If, as they hoped, they had struck down Great Britain, taken London, and compelled the payment of an enormous indemnity, why should they not seek to compel the cession of the different parts of the British Empire? It is the plainest and most obvious fact that Canada, fighting in France and Flanders, is fighting absolutely for the safety of Canada herself. No danger of invasion to Canada in a world war cataclysm such as this? Shall we take the position that we should not send our troops out of Canada, but allow the British fleet and our Allies to save us? Shall we take the position that we should not send our forces to help them, because constitutionally our forces should not be sent outside the Dominion unless to repel threatened invasion?
Could this country take that position? The defence of Canada! Where should that defence be conducted? That depends upon

circumstances; it might in some wars be strategically advantageous to defend Canada at the border, it might in others be strategically advantageous to defend Canada thousands of miles away, as we are doing it to-day. That is so plain, so obvious, to me that I marvel that any one should suggest that Canada's forces while fighting abroad are not fighting against the invasion of the sovereignty and autonomy of Canada.
The question has been raised whether it is constitutional for Canada to send forth her forces to defend herself in a place where she can best be defended-which, I say, is in France and Flandieirs. Well, Mr. Speaker, it is the first law of nations that they should protect themselves; it is the first duty of a government to its people to take any steps that may be necessary in defence of that people. But, it is said, we are widening the compulsion of the Militia Act. I agree entirely with those who have argued that we are not adopting any degree of compulsion that is not provided for in the legislation now on the statute-book. But it would not trouble me in the least degree if we were widening that compulsion. The first duty of this Government is to save the nation, to take such military steps as may be necessary to put the nation beyond danger from invasion in the war which threatens Canada and threatens the Empire. And I am confident that I speak for most of the members of this House when I say that the people of this country attach some importance to the British Empire and their connection with it-we are not only fighting for Canada, but fighting to maintain the integrity of the Empire which is threatened by German aggression. So that so far as the Militia Act is concerned, it does not concern me, and I believe it should not concern this House, whether it is narrower in its provisions than this Bill or not; the question before us is, from the standpoint of national safety, are we going to continue the war? I believe that the people of this country are determined to continue this war. For how long? Until, as I have said, it is won, and the Hohenzollern is overthrown.
It is said, or at least implied, that enough has been done, that the situation is such that further help on the part of Canada is not necessary. I wish I could say that that is true. I have pointed out that but little progress has been made upon that Western front, 'notwithstanding the outpouring of blood and of munitions. Today, we are confronted with as serious a situation as at any time since the outbreak of the war, except that, I believe, the Allies have now the offensive in the sense which we have not had it before. But we must remember, as pointed out by the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) that the effort of Russia has slackened. I hope that this condition will not continue. I believe that the welfare of Russia lies with the Allies, and that the people of Russia^ if properly led, will continue the great effort which they made from the outbreak of the war. I hope and pray that that may be so. But the fact is that the Russian offensive has slackened and that the German troops which are engaged upon that Eastern front are to-day in action on the Western front. And so the cry goes up for men, and more
men.	. . ,
That brings me to another point wnicn has been dwelt upon in this House and which cannot be dwelt upon too much the duty that we owe to those noble sons of Canada who have gone forward and are at the front to-day. Mr. Speaker, _ could Canada, or could any of Canada s citizens, con-aider seriously for a moment the desertion or abandonment of those men at the front? We have four divisions there; I visited them last November. I talked with officers going into their dugouts for the night. It was at a time when there had been great wastage in the ranks. There were men of ours in England whose training was not complete, and every effort was being made to hurry them forward to repair the casualties at the front. Officer after oflicer said to me:	I am going into the trenches tonight with seven hundred men where I ought to have a thousand men. I talked to both officers and men, and let me tell this House that if there is one thing which more than any other annoys the men at the front it is to read the headings in Canadian newspapers that are sent them that the war is going so well that it may soon be over. I tell this House that these men look back earnestly to this country for more and more reinforcements of their ranks. These men are daily walking hand in hand with death; the most earnest, the most noble band of men I have ever seen. I came away with a lump in my throat and with a great sense of my own uniworthiness. I wish that e very man in this House, French or English, could go to that front and see what these men are doing there. If that could be, I believe there would be no doubt as to how every man would vote upon this Bill. Canada, for her own honour and apart from

the question of her own safety and the safety of tne British Empire, must not desert these men at the front. We are on the ere of the greatest battles in the history of the world. Every effort will he put forth by the great nations engaged in this war to bring about a decision. Why? Because the wastage is eo great. It will he the strategy of commanders to press the war. This is why I say that we are on the eve of the greatest battles in the history of the world. There will be casualties, unfortunately, among the Canadians. How are we going to fill the gaps; how are we going to reinforce the ranks? The voluntary system has broken down; we must do what other nations have done, we must resort to compulsory military service. I believe that the people of Canada will say that if we desert these men at the front, God will desert this country. What do I mean by that? I mean that our moral fibre would deteriorate, that our national character would be broken, that in the eyes of the world and in the eyes of ourselves, we should aptpear as not having the manhood essential to a great nation.
Mr. Speaker, in what I have to say I would not wound the feelings of any man or woman in this country. 1 had hoped tfiat there might le unity respecting this Bill and I still hope that when this Bill is passed and becomes law, there will be unity on both sides of this House fn urging this country and all parts of it to respect that law. We talk about the necessity for food, for munitions, for supplies, and all these things are necessary; but if the people of Great Britain, of the United States and Canada devoted themselves to the production of food, munitions and supplies, who would hold the battle line at the front? The German is there, the German infantry, the German artillery ana they can only be defeated by human valour, by the men behind the lines who launch the fire of the artillery and the men in the trenches who scale the parapet, charge with bayonet and hand grenade and take the trenches of the Hun. You cannot win this war by encouraging agriculture, although that is necessary; you cannot win this war by mobilizing your railways, although that is necessary; the decision is to be got by human valour at the front and in no other way, although these other things are ancillary.
I will say just one more word about the volunteer system because the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) passed some strictures upon the Government in connection with its organization. The volunteer system was not only unjust but fSir Thomas White.]
it was illogical and in many ways it iin-peded the nation in putting forth its best effort in carrying on the war. Reference was made to myself and to my right hon. fi lend the Prime Minister as retarding recruiting. I do not believe that the members of this House; I do not'believe that the people of this country, realize, the burdens which devolve upon the ministers of the Government in time of war. Day and night, Sunday and Saturday, practically every week, there is the burden and the lesponsibility of the war. I mention that, not because we deserve any sympathy because our sacrifices and toil are as nothing compared with the sacrifices by the men who have gone to the front, and by the fathers, mothers and wives who have sent them forth. But notwithstanding the duties which have devolved upon us, notwithstanding the responsibilities with which we have been burdened, the members of this Government have done what they could within the limits of their physical powers to promote recruiting. The Prime Minister went from the Atlantic to the Pacific upon his return last fall appealing to large audiences throughout this country in a last effort to stimulate recruiting. For myself,
I have spoken upon scores of platforms in Ontario, at Montreal, and ,at Halifax in the interests of recruiting. Everything was done that could have been by the Government. All aid was afforded that was asked for by the Government and no nobler work was ever done by the devoted band of men and women who gave their time, thought and energy to the promotion of recruiting. I had hoped for the sake of unity, because I knew that this question would create division, that Canada, by the voluntary system, would have been able to carry on the war to the end which we all desire-victory. But it became apparent that the voluntary system was no longer effective. That was admitted by those men and women in this country who had devoted themselves to the work. It has been referred t.o by hon. members on both sides of this House who have given themselves day and night in aiding recruiting in their constituencies and elsewhere. The recruiting system broke down. The Government, for the safety of Canada and the Empire, and also for the honour of Canada, and in recognition of its obligation towards those men who have gone forward, brought down this Bill providing for compulsory military service. We all learn as this war progresses. War is a terrible realist; it brings you face to face with reality. It is a great discloses a great revealer; it reveals much

even to men whfl have been closest to the prosecution of this war. I believe that the bringing down of this compulsory military service Bill will do more to stimulate the national activities of Canada in all departments of life towards the prosecution of the war than anything that has happened before in the history of the war. Take the debates in this House; I have never heard such debates. I do not think that any man in this House has ever heard such speeches -speeches from the heart, sincere, a debate in which every man stands up and expresses his conviction to his fellow members in the desire to reach a right solution of this question and to determine what is the duty of Canada at this great crisis in our affairs. I respect the views that any of my fellow members put forward in this House. This is no time for partisanship; it is no time for antagonism. Sincerely and seriously we must consider the most important measure that, I think, was ever laid before this House and the effort on the part of the Government to meet a great national crisis. I have no fault to find with those who differ from me
But I have spoken because I desire, as others have done, to express my thoughts and convictions upon this question. I say that this country is in honour bound-no other course is open to us-to take such measures as will insure the continued and necessary reinforcement of our men at the front, and I believe that this debate will have great weight, in all parts of this community, in persuading people to that view. This is one of the great functions of Parliament. A debate of a week on a subject of this kind will do more to educate, enlighten and clarify public opinion than all the action that could be taken by individual members of the Government for a year.

I desire to say that this Bill must be passed by this Parliament. I believe that that is the will of the people of Canada. I believe that this Government can take no other course than that which we are now taking, if, in the words of one of the greatest orators of- the world, we are to have any regard for our past, or for our glory, or for the days that are to come.
Mr. PUGSLEY; Why not leave it as it is?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING AND ON THE AMENDMENTS.
speechtext:
I will come to that in a moment. This Bill will do more, not only to give us reinforcements for the men at the front, which is its immediate object, but to stir the moral enthusiasm of this people, to mobilize, and to organize the people of this country for war, than anything that has yet happened. I say the speeches in this House are not like the speeches delivered when we were discussing worn-out political formulas a little time ago. Men are speaking words of sincerity and truth from their hearts. That is one good result this debate has had. Let us rid this discussion of old worn-out issues, which are dead and gone. The thought of this world will never be the same,-the structure of society will never be the same again. This measure will not only give needed reinforcements, it will stimulate the people of this country, it will educate them on the great issues of the war, in a way they have never been educated before. No democracy, Mr. Speaker, ever puts forth its greatest effort until the religious sentiment of democracy is enlisted. My hon. friend smiles. Take the war of the Secession in the United States. Let my hon. friend read the second inaugural of Abraham Lincoln. Let him read Julia Ward Howe's " Battle Hymn of the Republic "-
Mine eyes have seen the glory of the coming of the Lord. He is trampling out the vintage where the grapes of wrath are stored.
The literature and ipoetry of that period breathes with religious fervour. You never get the strength of a democracy until, in addition to its material effort, there is put forth its spiritual effort. There must be self-sacrifice. There must be self-denial. There must be the mobilization of the spiritual energies of the nation. This Bill will do much to bring that about, because, if you are going to say to one man: You must offer up your life, men will realize, as never before, what sacrifice means, and will be prepared to support the Government in such action as may be necessary to bring the whole power of the nation to bear upon the problem of the prosecution of the war. This Bill will accomplish all these things.
*Referring to the remarks of the hon. gentleman from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), I am sorry I have to deal with matters which are only remotely relevant to the Bill, but which were put forward by him and seem to require some answer on my part. But my answer will be brief. I am



glad the hon. gentleman from South Renfrew made it clear this afternoon, with regard to the expression " conscription of wealth," which has been used a good deal by the newspapers of this country, since his bringing forward of the resolution which he read that he had not in mind conscription of capital. I may say to the House, and I would like to say to the press, but not for publication, that the use of the phrase " conscription of wealth " is leading to certain disturbing conditions in some parts of the community. I think it would be well, not to make use of a phrase which is not understood in its literal sense in this House, but to which some people outside may attach a meaning it is not intended to. bear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON MOTION FOR SECOND READING AND ON THE AMENDMENTS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) talked about equality of sacrifice,' and I am glad he made it clear that there is no equality of sacrifice, and there can be no equality of sacrifice between the ease of a man who gives his son and a man who writes a cheque for taxes. The two subjects should not be dealt with at the same time. They are separate and distinct. Mobilization of man-power, in order to reinforce our troops at the front, is one thing. Taxation for the purpose of finding funds for the prosecution of the war is another, and very different matter. It is perfectly proper for any member of this House to say to me on a proper occasion, say on the Budget debate, or in Supply, "you are not raising sufficient money by taxation; you are raising too much by loan." That is a fair argument, when we are dealing with the subject of finance, but it is not a pertinent argument, I submit, in this debate. It is not relevant, because you are comparing things which are essentially different, when you say that, if there is conscription of man-power, there must be also conscription of wealth. I think, however, .that, when the people of the community are in the condition that they are in to-day, under strain, stress and affliction, a good effect is produced if they realize that others, who may not be sending sons or husbands to the front, at all events are contributing,or are made to contribute, of their substance to. the prosecution of the war.
I ask this House to hear this also in mind: besides giving due attention to the providing of money by loans and by taxation for the prosecution of the.war, the Minister of Finance must not lose sight of the fact that if he attempts too much, he will defeat 
his own purpose. In other words, taxation must be wisely imposed. Men who are reputed to .be wealthy may have no ready cash. Let us say that they are engaged in a great industry which employs thousands of men; shall the state seize any portion of the capital invested in that industry? The state cannot pay its debts in kind; it must pay in cash. The financing of a war must be carried on by drawing from the liquid funds of the nation-from that and the new wealth, so to speak, created during the war; otherwise essential industry is likely to suffer. The Minister of Finance, therefore must be sagacious in his imposition of taxation, or he may defeat the very purpose, laudable though it may be, that he has in view.
The member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) said that what he really had in mind was an income tax. There is a good deal to be said for an income tax. It is a fair form of taxation, because it does not take away from a man what he really needs. But it must be borne in mind that if you have too severe an income tax, you do impair the liquid capital of the community which is available for loans and for the purposes of banking and commerce. Canada has never lacked money since this war began. We speak of the man behind the gun, but, so far as Canada is concerned, the dollar has always been behind the man-and that is the position to-day. There has been abundance of money to send our men forward and to maintain them at the front, and to finance Great Britain in her purchase of needed munitions and supplies in Canada. All those moneys have been found by the Government., It is open to hon. gentlemen opposite to say to me:	you have not raised as much as
you should by taxation; you should have raised more by .taxation and less by loans. That would be a fair and pertinent argument to-put forward-though I would controvert it-but not in connection with this Bill. Can you weigh the imponderable? Can you put a human life on one scale and a million dollars on .the other? The measure of taxation which I brought down to this House, and which was objected to by 'the member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) as being tom severe, was one of the stiffest measures of taxation ever brought down in any country. The member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) the other night put on Hansard some figures .as to .the amount contributed by the largest taxpayers. I stated that if the war went on we should prob-

bably have an in-come tax. I will not spare the people from taxation, if taxation is necessary in order to win the war. At the outset I taxed the financial institutions; I imposed special war taxation. By the end of this fiscal year we shall have raised nearly $200,000,000 by special war taxation. But in our direct taxation I have resorted chiefly to those who have derived advantage from the war. We said to them: if you have made abnormal profits through war conditions, you must give a large proportion of them to the State. I submit that that was an absolutely sound course. Such taxation is much fairer than an income tax, especially in Canada, for ''this reason: in Ontario, let us say, you may have a tax upon incomes by the municipality, a tax upon incomes by the province and a similar tax imposed by the Federal authorities. Another thing that I have always tried to keep in mind is this: the war will be over some day. This country has been inviting people to come into it from all parts of the world-from the United States and from Europe. When men are invited to come into a country they naturally ask, what are the conditions in that country? Any Minister of Finance who is considering a taxation scheme in Canada must have regard also to taxation in the United States. If your taxation is too severe, it will have the effect of driving some men out of the country and preventing others from coming in. That argument was submitted to me in connection with the excess business profits tax and there is something to be said for it. It is true that in war time it may be necessary to raise money to meet the needs of the war, even though immigration or capital may temporarily cease to flow into the country. I am not rejecting an income tax. This war has gone on much longer than any of us ever thought. We have taken, step by step, measures .necessary to find money with which to back the men at the front. We will continue to take those steps, to issue loans, to impose taxation, as severe as may be necessary in order that our troops may have financial backing and support. This Government may be depended upon to bring in such measures of taxation as may be necessary to accomplish that end. An hon. gentleman suggested the other day that I was not taxing wealth sufficiently, and that there was a motive behind my action in that regard. I can tell that hon. gentleman that I have made many enemies, through no fault of my own, on account of 165i
the severe taxation which has been imposed. But that is absolutely of no consequence. We will take whatever measures are necessary, whether by income tax, succession duty tax, a tax upon real estate, or otherwise, in order that we may win this war. But I qualify that to this extent: taxation should not be imposed for the purpose of punishing anybody. Taxation should be wisely imposed, and only to the extent necessary. Good judgment is required as to the taxation which a nation should be asked to stand during war time. Having regard to the high cost of living, in Canada and other places, you must be very careful in coming to a decision concerning the imposition of an income tax upon people of moderate incomes.
Let me tell the House what has brought about the agitation with regard to the so-called conscription of wealth. The record, of' this country since the beginning of the war has been wonderful, not only in respect of the number of men who have gone forward,, offering their lives., if necessary, for their country; but in. respect also of the amounts: of money liberally -subscribed to the Patriotic Fund, the Bed Cross and other funds. One of the glories of this country will be its voluntary effort in support of those funds. The hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) said the other day that $40,000,000 had been raised or pledged in connection with those funds: Let us not overlook that; but unfortunately, in every community, there are one or two or three or mpre men who are rich and who are close and who have not contributed to those funds, and the people of this country feel that they should be made to contribute. If I can make them contribute, I will do so. I am not sure that it would not be well, in connection with an income tax, if we Drmg one down, to provide that a man shpuld be exempted to the extent, that he has contributed to the Patriotic and the Bed Cross Funds, because, if you impose too severe taxation, you will tend t.o stop-I do not say you will stop-the voluntary flow of funds for those great purposes, and it is not only the money that is valuable, but the good will. The heart that is behind the offering tp those funds is of priceless advantage to the people of Canada in the prosecution of this war.
I shall not speak upon the referendum -the expedient put forward by the leader of the Opposition, except to say that I agree with the arguments which have been put forth by thpse on his own side against the course which he has suggested. I will not

say a referendum is unconstitutional, but I do not believe that the abstract question-are you or are you not in favour of [DOT]conscription?-will get a fair decision on the part of the people of this country on this most momentous question. The public, as has been said by the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) requires leadership. You could not get the people of this country properly to pronounce upon that question if submitted by referendum unless you have practically the equivalent of a general election in which men would discuss the issue and speak out of their hearts to the hearts .of the people. There would have to be the tumult and excitement of a general election which is greatly to be deprecated at this time. 'There is one rule for individuals, one rule for Governments, and the Government that adopts that rule, like the individual that adopts, that rule, will always be on safe ground. What is the rule? To do the right thing, the noble thing, the-patriotic thing. What is the right thing, and the noble thing and the patriotic thing at this time? To take such measures as may be necessary to prosecute this war to a victorious conclusion, and to support those gallant men of ours, our noblest and our best, who to-day are fighting for you and for me on the battlefields of Europe. They are fighting just as much in the defence of 'Canada as if they were fighting on the shores of Nova 'Scotia or along the banks of the St. Lawrence.
I realize that there is a sharp cleavage of opinion upon this question, and I have endeavoured to discuss it in such a fashion as to wound no man's feelings. I am sure the House will give me credit when I say that we members respect each other's convictions. While we differ sharply upon questions of national importance, we yet respect each other and we speak what we have to say without heat, without hostility, without enmity. Looking at this matter from the standpoint of the statesman, I ask: What of the future? It has been pointed out and emphasized here that there is a cleavage of opinion in this country. My opinion is that this debate in this Hous.e may go a long way towards assisting the carrying out of this measure, because I believe one of the functions, of Parliament, in debating great questions like this, is to inform the public, to persuade them of the expediency of a certain course. This Bill will pass into law. In my administrative position, and in any debates in which I have taken part in this House, I have treated all members on both sides of the

House, no matter of what nationality, only as Canadians; I do not know them as French or English; they are my fellow-Canadians. For 200 years or more ourselves and our fathers and our forefathers have lived together in this country. There have been differences of opinion; sometimes there has been discord; once there was civil war, rebellion; but on the whole we have got on fairly well together. We have been engaged in the great work of reducing half a continent to the use -of civilization. We respect each other in this House, and I believe the different sections of this country respect each other, although they have their differences. I believe the . right thing to do is to pass this Bill. I believe compulsory military service is necessary in this country. How can we secure practical union in support of this measure? We shall not get it by taunting eaph otheT, by political recrimination, by reviving old differences of opinion; but if hon. members on both sides of the House, the leaders, the front-benchers and all other members, after the debate is over, would join in asking the people of this country to respect the obligation of this measure and to assist the Government in putting it into effect and carrying it out, that would make for unity in this country, and I believe that could be done. This Bill must be enacted into law because it is necessary for the national safety and honour that it should be enacted into law. Let us all, French and English, in this House and in this country, accept this Bill as being a necessary measure, having regard to the grave national conditions which beset us, and in that way let us have unity; let us present the appearance of unity to the world. I do not believe insuperable difficulties would present themselves if we all address ourselves to the matter, and I leave that thought for the consideration of this House.'

THE TORONTO, HAMILTON & BUFFALO RAILWAY.
House in Committee-Mr. Blain in the Chair-on Bill No. 39, respecting the Toronto, Hamilton and Buffalo Railway.-Mr. T. J. Stewart.

I beg to move that clauses 1 and 2 be struck out of the Bill,

and that the Bill be then reported and given its third reading.
Explain.

This Bill has reference to an agreement made between the town of Dundas and the Hamilton and Dun-das Street Railway Company in regard to the handling of freight by the electric road. Dundas is situated in a valley and as the steam roads do not go in there, the Hamilton & Dundas Street Railway Company entered into an agreement with the Toronto, Hamilton and Buffalo Railway Company to handle the freight over the electric road. There was a clause in the agreement that if the town of Dundas saw fit to pass a bylaw extending the charter for 29 years, making a total of 50 years, and ratification sought from the Ontario Legislature. The town of Dundas passed the bylaw and got special legislation by the Ontario Legislature ratifying the agreement. The ratification could not apply to the Toronto, Hamilton and Buffalo Railway Company as they were under Dominion charter. The Toronto, Hamilton and Buffalo Company are now asking the Dominion Government to place them in the same position as the town of Dundas. The town of Dundas say "No, we are not going to allow that." They take the ground that the freight cars were allowed to remain in front of thfe people's doors on the streets of Dundas, which is most unfair; but the Toronto, Hamilton and Buffalo Company has no control whatever over the streets. Wishing to be fair, however, we agreed to spend $15,000 on a new switching, ground and freight lines. Then they took the objection that the smoke was a nuisance, and that we would have to handle the freight by electric power. That meant buying two motors at a cost of $80,000. The interest on that would be $4,800 and the total earnings of the road are only $5,400 a year. The Toronto, Hamilton and Buffalo Company therefore could not see their way to handling the freight by electric power at that enormous cost. We do not think a little town like Dundas with only 5,000 people had any right to ask for something no other place in the Dominion had got. We agreed, however, to having legislation put through placing us under the Dominion Railway Board. That ' apparently did not satisfy them. The Railway Committee amended the Bill to read 5 years instead of 29. To my mind the committee could do only one of two things: either grant the 29 years, or say: No, they had no right whatever to male the agreement without all parties being represented at the meeting. We have made up our minds that if the town of Dundas will not grant us what we think we are entitled to, we will withdraw these two clauses and let the town handle the freight as it sees fit.

This Bill was thoroughly discussed before the Railway Committee, representatives being present from the town of Dundas and the surrounding district. I am sorry the hon. member for Wentworth, who is particularly interested in this Bill, is not present. I am sure he would take serious objection to the Bill being amended in this way. Many of us who were present at the meetings of the Railway Committee are strongly opposed to the wishes of the railway representatives, who are simply trying to get their charter, which has now only one year to run, extended for 29 years. Has the hon. member for Hamilton given notice of this amendment?

I am acting on the advice of the Law Clerk of the House. I am given to understand that the committee had no right to amend the Bill for five years; they should either have made it 29 years or refused. We certainly do not intend to accept the Bill as amended. Therefore, why should there be any objection to allowing us to withdraw these two clauses? We have some rights in the matter. I think we have been treated most unfairly. We are simply asking for what the town of Dundas took for themselves, and I think we should get it. I have stated the facts exactly as they are, and I now ask the committee to allow me to withdraw clauses 1 and 2 of the Bill. That will only leave in the Bill clauses 5 and 6. Clause 5 refers to freight arrangements with the-Michigan Central Railroad Company, the Canada Southern Railway Company, and the Grand Trunk Railway Company. Clause-6 empowers the company to hold stock in a. steamboat company. These two clauses: have already been passed by the committee.
Probably we should make better progress if we allowed the Bill to stand until the hon. member for Wentworth was present.
He knows I am proposing to withdraw these two clauses; we have talked it over.
But he is not here.
Is it not customary, Mr. Chairman, that notice be given of an amendment of this kind?
