; . MILITARY SERVICE ACT, 1917.
Consideration of the proposed motion of Sir Robert Borden for the second reading of Bill No. 75, Military Service Act, 1917, and [DOT]of the amendments thereto, resumed.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on the Bill 'before the House, I think I fully appreciate the importance of the departure we are proposing to take in reference to the enlistment of soldiers. My hon. friend (Mr. [DOT]Graham), who preceded me, declared that he was not going to recriminate or criticise. Eor my part, I am going to take the liberty of offering some criticism, and if that is called recrimination, then I am going to recriminate.
In the first place, I do not think that the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), in introducing this Bill gave us as ample information as he might have given. For instance, he might have told us whether Great Britain had required of this country men rather than more production. We have seen a great deal in the newspapers on the subject of production, and the other day we had the report from the recently-appointed food controller of England that it was absolutely necessary to have production from this country and from the United States to supply Great Britain. Had the Prime Minister told us how much production on our part Great Britain needed, we should have had a better idea of how many men could be spared from this country. I quite understand that it would not have been possible for Great Britain to tell us how many men they would like us to send,
IMr. Stewart]
for the reason that, I suppose, this will depend entirely upon the progress of the war. On that point I doubt that the Prime Minister could have given us much more information than he did. But the right hon. gentleman can easily see that the quantity of food that can be produced in this country for use in Great Britain will depend very largely on how many men we send to the front. It must be borne in mind that we are a very sparse population. I do not agree with those who say that voluntary enlistment has failed. It may have fallen short of the number of men required, but in my judgment it has certainly not failed. According to the last return there have been 421,767 enlistments in this country. To enlist this number in a country with a population of about 7,500,000, spread over an area about 3,000 miles long and perhaps 1,000 miles broad, besides keeping up agriculture and other industries, as well as the professions of the country, I think is doing wonderfully well; it says a great deal for the patriotism of the people of Canada.
Now, so far as the voluntary enlistment can be said to have failed, I cannot but blame the Government very greatly for that state of affairs. My hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) pointed out some of the mistakes that had been made by the Government. He referred to the discussion reported in the press as having taken place between the ex-Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes) and the other members of the Government on the necessity or otherwise of continuing enlistment, and pointed out that this had had a bad effect. But that which had the worst effect in Ontario, at any rate in my judgment, was that the press was full of rumours of over expenditure, graft and corruption. There were the charges made here in the House and the investigations that followed. There was a feeling abroad, which was reflected in the newspapers, that the Government was spending quite unnecessarily enormous sums of money.
In some sections of the country the Government enlisted men and kept them for months in this country after which they were discharged as medically unfit. A great many others were taken over to England and there discharged as medically un- . fit. The ordinary man, the farmer and the working man, understands the expense that is incurred in a proceeding of that kind. The people got discouraged with the general condition of the country resulting largely from the fact that the Government

was practically doing nothing. There is no doubt that my hon. friend from South Renfrew was correct when he said that the Government did not take an actiye part in the enlistment campaign that was going on throughout the country. In a great many instances they sent big, husky fellows, captains, majors or something of that kind, drawing anywhere from $6 to $10 a day, around telling the boys in the towns and the country that they should enlist and go to the front.

Were not these men who were taking part in recruiting, men who had returned wounded from the front? I could give the hon. gentleman several names of recruiting officers who had been wounded -at the front.

I was just coming to that if my hon. friend had not got impatient. There were many men who never went to the front, who never saw the front and who never intended going to the front, big, husky fellows drawing large salaries, and these very officers are trying to enlist men at the present time. Would not a wounded returned soldier be the right man to go around and address recruiting meetings? A man standing on the platform who had been at the front and had been wounded could say: Go and do as I have done. I am sure he would have a great deal more influence on the audience than the fellow who has never been at the front, who is within the age, who is perfectly capable of going to the front, who is drawing a salary as captain or major, dictating to the men down below him in the audience and telling them that they should go to the front? Naturally, they say: "Why does he not go instead of telling us to go?" In many other ways this Government discouraged voluntary enlistment. But the main discouragement was the appearance in the press of reports of the enormous and unnecessary expenditures which have been carried on in connection with the war and enlistment. The people, I confess, thoughout Ontario at any rate, were very patriotic and loyal; they subscribed an enormous amount of money for carrying on the war. Another thing that, in my judgment, influenced voluntary enlistment was that there was a campaign carried on for munition workers. A great many men said that it was just as necessary to have munition workers as it was to have men at the front. I know that the papers were filled with that sort of talk. Was there ever anything more preposterous, more absolutely absurd, than to put it
abroad that it was just as necessary to have men making munitions in this country as it was to have men going to the front to fight our battles? Munition workers got from $2.50 to $8 a day, while a man for going to the front was paid -$1.10, with a certain amount for field allowances, clothes and his separation allowance. You cannot possibly figure that up to be more than $2.25 a day, and he was expected to risk his life. Yet the munition worker was getting anywhere from $2.50 to $8 a day, and a great many people said that it was just as patriotic to make munitions as it was to go to the front. I leave it to any man here to say if that was not an absurd statement to be put through the length and breadth of this country and to be uttered from public platforms. There was an advertising campaign carried on in the principal newspapers in Toronto for munition workers as if the men making munitions could not advertise for their men and could not get men just as well as any Government official that the Lord ever produced.
Does he produce them?

Were they not just as capable of getting their own men as were the Government? I understand that $60,000 was paid in connection with this munition workers' campaign. I know that in making that statement I am speaking within the mark, because I know something about it. That also hurt voluntary enlistment, because people became disgusted with the way in which the money of this country was being spent for so-called assistance in the war when it was not for assistance in the war.

Has the hon. gentleman ever asked a question in this House, or has a minister ever made the statement that the hon. gentleman has just made, that $60,000 of the Dominion's money had been spent in advertising for workers for munition factories? That is the statement that the hon. gentleman made, and I challenge the truth or correctness of it.
I do not care what my hon. friend challenges. I am telling him the truth. I imagine I can get as many people to believe me as the hon. gentleman can get to believe him.

I asked the hon. gentleman if he had ever asked the question in this House, or has it ever been asked5 As a test of the bona fides and good faith

of the hon. gentleman, let him ask the question now and see what truth there is in the statement.

My hon. friend beside me says there is a return to that effect, tout I do not care a cent whether there is or not; I know. I do not care whether they bring down a return or not, and it is not necessary to ask the question in the House, because I know it myself.
That was for your own 'friend, the Boss rifle.

I have nothing to do with the Boss rifle. My hon. friend cannot chuck the Boss rifle at me, because I had nothing to do with it. I have given some of the reasons why voluntary enlistment has stop.ped to a certain extent. But, last month there were over 7,200 men enlisted, and if you will take the return which was brought down in this House very recently you will notice that for the last three months more men enlisted than there was wastage at the front.
Has the hon. gentleman any information as to how many of those men who enlisted last month were for the infantry, or the fighting line?

No, but I might tell my hon. friend that when they do enlist for one branch they are sometimes sent to another branch when they get to England, so that it will be pretty hard to tell what they are in now. I know men who enlisted in the artillery, and who, when they got to England, were put into the infantry, in spite of a very strong protest from their families at home. That brings me to the question of enlistment from Quebec. My hon. friend finds fault with that enlistment. I am sorry to say that it is a ease, to a large extent, of chickens coming home to roost. It is said that if you sow with the wind, you will reap with the whirlwind. My earnest hope is that my hon. friends will not do the reaping accqrding to that adage. The first time the so-called Nationalist movement in Quebec was brought to my attention was in the Drummond-Arthabaska byelection. It has been frequently stated on the floor of this House, and not denied by my Conservative friends, that they were at the bottom of the movement and endorsed the Nationalist candidate in that election. They were behind the extremists in Quebec, when they told the people that they owed nothing to Great Britain. In that election, my Conservative friends were accused, time

and again, of endorsing the man who made these speeches. It is certainly true that they endorsed the Nationalists in the election of 1911.
Will the hon. members kindly explain the difference to-day in the platform of Bourassa and the Nationalists, and the platform of my hon. friend's leader in this House? .

Where are they
now?

Where they have always been. My comrades from Quebec are absolutely as honest in their views to-night as my hon. friend who has interrupted me. After all, though we differ on this occasion, it is not necessary to say a man is dishonest in his view.
Will the hon. gentleman deny that the Nationalists are now on the same side as himself and his honoured leader?
Wait till the first vote is taken on your partner's motion.

'My hon. friend from
Renfrew has answered the hon. gentleman, but personally I absolutely deny that there is any collusion between my hon. leader and his supporters from Quebec or the supporters of my hon. friend on that side from that province. But in that election there was the usual collusion of my honourable friends in sharp practices. Both in politics and in business such collusion will come to naught. My view has always been since I was a boy, that there is only one way to do business or politics, and that is to be absolutely honest. You may succeed by chicanery for a little while, but it meets with poor success, and the chicanery of my hon. friends in the Drum-mond-Arthabaska election, and in the election of 1911, did more harm to this country than they can imagine, and now it is reacting on them. Perhaps it was smart practice at the time, but honesty is the best policy in politics and in business. My hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) gave the Bill credit for the organization of labour. I asked him the question where he found it, and he told me he thought it was there. The only language that could be construed in that way at all would be the last section of the interpretation clause, which reads:
And whereas, by reason of the large number of men who have already left agricultural and industrial pursuits in Canada to join such Expeditionary Force as volunteers, and of the necessity of sustaining under such conditions the productivity of the Dominion, it is expedient to secure the men still required, not by ballot as provided in the Militia Act, but by selective draft.
No, there is nothing in that to show there is any intention to organize labour in this country. The Bill expresses the intention of selecting men for military purposes, but nothing to show there is any intention lor the organization of labour-at least, I say so.
That brings me to the question of voluntary enlistment versus conscription. The one great benefit of voluntary enlistment, in my view, is that, after all, the man, whoever he may be, voluntarily goes to the front and voluntarily risks his life. Against that, for compulsory conscription, there is the basic theory that it is the duty of every man to defend his country. If you start on that basis, I am free to confess that the only logical conclusion you can come ta is conscription, whether it be selective or otherwise, whether it be according to the Militia
Act or according to the proposed Bill No. 75. But, after all, the difficulty with me is that I dislike to say that anybody else shall do something if I will not do it myself. I confess that I shrink from saying to any man or woman that his or her eon shall go to the front and expose his life in war when I am not going myself. Hon. gentlemen know that under this Bill I would not be selected for military service, because I am too old, by many years. That made me hesitate; it took me a long -time to make up my mind-because I do not try to be generous at the expense of my wife's relations. I ratl er felt that, as a representative of the people, I was putting myself in a position of dictatorship. Although I am represented in the military service by the only member of my family who cpuld possibly volunteer, I myself am not at the front, and I hesitated to say that any other man's son should go, especially when he might never come back. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that that is a serious position for me to take. But, as I have said, every man is required to defend his country when the time comes. There seems to be only one way of ensuring the proper defence of the country at this time, and that is by means of conscription. But any measure of compulsory service must be fairly and properly carried out. A great many people-not especially the people whom I represent-but people to whom I have talked on and off the trains, have asserted that ever since the war started the business connected with the war has been carried on by the Government in a most partisan manner. That has hurt recruiting in Ontario worse than anything else. In my constituency-or, rather, in the constituency that I am supposed to represent-a good many more Liberals than Conservatives volunteered.

Does the hon.
member mean Liberal officers?

No, I mean men. My
hon. friend knows that there would not be more Liberal officers. T have no complaints of that kind to make. To do the Government and the Department of Militia justice, I may say that the department has freely done everything in reason that I have asked it to do since the war started. I must give them that credit.
Why, then, do you say that there was partisanship in your county?

I did not say that there was partisanship in my county. My hon.

friend is very clever to-night; what is the matter with him? In the first place, I do not own a county. In the next place, I did not say that partisanship was evidenced in the district that I represent. So far as I know, it certainly was not.
Hear, hear.

But I did say that the feeling was abroad in the country that partisanship had been exercised by the Government ever since the war started. For instance, have any Liberals been given positions on the numerous and innumerable commissions that have been appointed?
The Pensions Commission.
Not that I know of.

One of the officers now on the Pensions Commission was one of the most intolerable and intolerant Grits in my town. If every hon. gentleman will frankly admit what he himself knows, then the public will get the truth.
Who is this intolerable Grit to whom my hon. friend refers? I suppose he was intolerable to my hon. friend because my hon. friend was intolerable to him.
A man named McKeaud.
On the Pensions Commission?
On the Pensions Commission-a good office.
There is no such man on the Pensions Commission that I know of.
You do not know everything.
I understand that the Pensions Commission consists of Mr. Ross, Mr. Todd and Mr. Labatt.
I did not say that he was one of the commissioners; I said that he was on the Pensions Commission.

Oh, he got into a clerkship, I suppose. You should never have allowed him to get that clerkship; you had better dismiss*him.
Mr. LAlLOR: It surely was not partisanship that induced the Government to send Colonel Andrew Thompson, of Ottawa, into my county to take charge of a battalion that had already been recruited.
Why should he not go?
I say that he was not sent there because of partisanship.
My hon. friend is quite willing that Colonel Andrew Thompson should go overseas and risk his life at the front. I do not know if there is anything-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I direct the attention of hon. gentlemen to the fact that there are entirely too many interjections? Hon. memibers ought to extend to the House the courtesy of rising if they wish to make remarks.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker; I was not getting into trouble. I never noticed that my hon. friends were desirous of stopping any Liberals from going to the front.. They have always been perfectly willing that Liberals should go to the firing line, and I suppose they will continue to be.
Nonsense.
As my hon. friend says, why not?
Oh, no; I said "nonsense."

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

In introducing this Bill the Prime Minister said that the Militia Act, vrhich has been on the statute book for many years, did not provide for the proper selection of men for military service. I refer hon. gentlemen to section 27 of the Militia Act, which is as follows:-
When men are required to organize or complete a' corps at any time, either for training or for an emergency, and enough men do not volunteer to complete the quota required, the men liable to serve shall be drafted by ballot; hut at no time shall more than one son belonging to the same family residing in the same house, if there are more than one inscribed on the Militia roll, be drawn, unless the number of names so inscribed is insufficient to complete the required proportion of service men.
Nothing in this Bill, so far as I know, provides for such selection as is provided for in that section of the Militia Act. Nothing in this Bill allows selection, except according to the discretion of the tribunal appointed for the purpose. Without desiring to throw out any reflection, I may say that this tribunal will be appointed by hon. gentlemen opposite. There is nothing in the Bill to indicate how the selections shall be made; there is nothing in it which provides for any organization of labour.
I have pointed out that the militia workers, for whom advertisements were floated

about in the newspapers, were paid from $2.50 to $8 a day, whereas the man who went to fight was paid $1.10 a day, besides being maintained and furnished with equipment. It is the duty of this country to pay the man who has actually to go to the front better than he has been paid. There is absolutely no comparison between the duties a man working in a militia factory performs and in the duties a man going to the front performs, and why men should be asked to go to the front for $1.10 a day, including equipment and maintenance, when a man working in a militia factory received from $2.50 to $8 a day, is more than I can comprehend and is aBsolutely unfair. The Minister of Finance said this afternoon that there was plenty of money for the support of the men at the front. The Government, therefore, should take steps now to pay our fighting men more than they are receiving at present.
Can the hon. member fix any amount of pay per day which he thinks would be commensurate with the sacrifices incurred and the risks taken by the men at the front?

Certainly not, but does that prevent us from paying them a reasonable remuneration? It would take a great deal of money, but there are a great many people in this country to share the burden. The men at the front enlisted for patriotic purposes; they did not enlist for the sake of the pay, but that is no reason why we should not give them a reasonable remuneration. Is it?
No. [DOT]

Then we absolutely agree. That brings me to the question of taxation which the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) touched upon this afternoon. The Minister of Finance this afternoon made an admirable speech, with which I cannot possibly find any fault excepting that he emphasized the fact that we have as much need for effort now as we ever had before. Surely such a statement was unnecessary. Any one in this country over five years old who reads about the war knows that it is absolutely necessary to make as much effort now as it was before. Then the minister, discussing the objections taken by some hon. members on this side of the House to the Bill, discussed the question: Shall we not send troops outside of Canada? There is no question as to whether we should send troops outside of
Canada or not; the question is as to the methods of raising troops, whether by vol-untarysm or by conscription, to send to the front; at least, that is my understanding of the arguments presented on this side of the House. The Minister of Finance also stated that the voluntary system had failed in England, and he quoted the Conscription Bill there. The minister must bear in mind that the English people, before bringing conscription into force, organized labour and industry in
9 p.m. England. That is the difference between this country and England. I am not going to discuss what the minister should do in regard to taxation; but while the minister has taxed wisely in many waye, I have never agreed with his blanket increase of 7J per cent, and he will notice that while the United States complimented him to the extent of saying they were going to do likewise, they afterwards did not do so. Every one in this country, no matter whether he is rich or ordinarily well off, or in whatever financial condition he may be, will have to pay more taxes on account of the war. We cannot continue to borrow. I think we have paid $100,000,000 towards the expenditures of the war. Am I correct in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This year we paid $60,000,000 on account of principal. So far as I know, only ourselves and Great Britain are paying towards the principal of war expenditure.

What the other fellow does, does not help us. The capital debt in the United States is very small in comparison with its population and-resources, so that that country can well afford to borrow, a few billions of dollars and still not have a large capital debt. We, however, cannot do that, and moreover, we have no means of securing the money, because if we borrow too much, we check the. commercial development of the country, and we cannot afford to do that. At the present time we cannot borrow from the United States; we have made several large domestic loans, and there is a limit to such borrowings. Therefore, while I do not say that we should pay all the expenses of the war as it progresses, we must pay more of the war expenditure as we go along, and we must tax every one regardless of whether he is rich or not. I have no faith in that catch-phrase-conscription of wealth-that one hears everywhere throughout the country. I have asked many people what they mean by "conscription of wealth," but nine

out of ten, in fact, ten out of ten, cannot tell me what they mean. We must tax wealth, and probably what the people mean by "conscription of wealth," is that we should impose an income tax. The Minister of Finance will have to resort to an income tax, although he has told us time and again that the expense of collecting an incodie tax will be very great. I appreciate that fact; but we have to form a basis for the taxation of wealth, and in my judgment, we shall have to resort to the imposition of an income tax; indeed, I would not he surprised if we had to resort to a land tax, because we have to tax the people of this country in such a way that they will feel it. The minister spoke this afternoon very eloquently about what discussion in this House would do towards organizing the people. We, as a Parliament, must organize the people, and the minister must tax the people so that every one will _feel that he is doing something towards this war, .as every one has a right to do.
I object to the regulations, with reference to the guidance of the tribunals that select the men, being made by Order in Council. The Parliament of Canada is the place where such regulations should be made. It is all very well for the Government to ask us to trust them, and to say that they will not exhibit partyism in these tribunals; but the Government has shown partyism from the very start of the war. They must remember that they have done so, and therefore they must remember that in the ordinary Liberal mind there is a suspicion -that perhaps should not be there, but that is still there-and all that the Liberals I know of want is fair play in this selection. The suspicion in their minds is that they will not receive fair play if these regulations are made by Order in Council. I do not think I have anything more to say at the present time with reference to the backsliding^ of my hon. friends on the other side of the House.
I come now to the question of the war. It does not matter to me particularly whether this Government have done what they should have done since the war started. It does not matter to me particularly, except as a citizen, whether they do what is right in the future or not, but my duty is plain. I am only answerable for myself and on this question, as on every other, my conscience must be absolutely clear!
I am in no way responsible for the sins of the Government; I am not responsible for anything they have done in the past or may do in the future.

We are at war. The leaders of the two great parties have both declared that we are in the war to the last man and the last dollar, and the press of the country have declared the same thing. Our men are fighting at the front and they have to be supported. Apparently voluntary enlistment has fallen down. No matter whose the fault, it certainly has slackened up within the last five or six months; the men required are not coming forward. In view of the slaughter that is going on at the front we do not know how many men will be required, and .if we are going to act on the principle that it is the duty of every man to defend his country there is nothing else for us to do but to pass this Bill. Voting according to my conscience, being left absolutely free to do so by my right hon. leader, I shall support the Bill on its second reading. On the third reading I shall vote according to my conscience again, and I reserve the right to vote for or against the Bill according to the improvements that may be made in it in committee, and according ,to what concurrent legislation may be introduced in the way of taxation, the organization of labour exclusive of manpower for the front, and the organization of industry. I should not like to .suggest an election, as did my hon. friend from Saskatoon (Mr. McCraney). If I might suggest anything to hon. gentlemen opposite it would be this; in place of a referendum that when this Bill passes they close up this legislature for a couple of weeks or a month, for the purpose of forming not a coalition government, but a coalition of-both Houses of Parliament in one grand effort to get 'the necessary men for the front by voluntary enlistment. I say that because I cannot help feeling that a grave responsibility rests upon the people of this country, and unless something of this kind be done there is likely to be produced in this country a disunion that must last for a considerable number of years. While I believe that conscription is the proper basis, it being every man's duty -to serve his country, at the same time I most strongly urge that both sides of this House and 'both Houses of Parliament get together for two weeks in one grand effort to get the necessary men by voluntary enlistment, and if I might say so, I think my hon. friends from the province of Quebec could well join in such a campaign, and I hope they will do so. I believe such an effort would bring unity throughout the length and breadth of this land. Unity perhaps is not so important as winning the

war, but next to winning the waT the most important thing to this country is to have the people of all the provinces of this Dominion united. I thank you, Mr. Speaker.

I understood my hon.
friend in the earlier part of his remarks to make a statement t.o the effect that the Dominion Government had expended $60,000 in an advertising campaign for munitions workers. I am sure my hon. friend would not wish to have any statement of his that was inaccurate go out to the country, and I wish to say for the Government that I believe there is absolutely no basis for such a statement. I felt so at the time, but to make sure I called up the Deputy Minister of Militia, and he tells me that absolutely no such expenditure was made through that department; and I do not see how it could very well have been made through any other department.

My information comes
from the man who got the contract. The minister will possibly say that it was English money that was being spent.
If the Munitions Board spent that sum of money in an advertising campaign, it had absolutely nothing to do with this Government; it was not our money.
That is only a subterfuge.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not at all.
Mr. NBSBI'TT:	Who pays the money
eventually?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The British Government.

Do not we have to pay
our proportion of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If we lend any money to the British Government here for the expenditures of the Imperial Munitions Board, it is a set-off to money which the Imperial Government advances to us for expenditures in Great Britain and on the Continent. It is just as much the money of the Imperial Government when our cheque passes to the Imperial Munitions Board, as my hon. friend's money is his own. This Government, is not in any way responsible, and has no authority whatsoever over the expenditures of the Imperial Munitions Board.

I quite appreciate that, but when the grand. settlement is made in the end, do not we have to pay our proportion of the expenditures that have been
made for getting munitions for our men at the front?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In virtue of an arrangement which has been made, we pay the Imperial Government a certain amount in respect of the maintenance of our men at the front and the munitions which our troops use. But the policy of the Imperial Munitions Board is not necessarily the policy of this Government. I do not think my hon. friend would say that we have responsibility where we have no authority.

I only mentioned that point as one of the reasons for the failure of voluntary enlistment. If the minister says that this expenditure concerns the Munitions Board alone, I have nothing more to say, but undoubtedly we shall have to pay our proportion of it when the final settlement comes. I have not the remotest intention of wishing to mislead the people of this country. I know my information is absolutely correct, because I got it from the man who took the contract.

Mr. Speaker, there are occasions when .it is difficult for memlbers of this House to decide what is the best course to pursue'. I quite understand that the legislation now before us is causing a good many to have doubts as to what is their proper course. Speaking for myself, however, my path of duty lies perfectly clear before me in the support of the measure the Government has [DOT]brought down. Never have I seen a great measure brought before the House that I could support with so good a conscience, or with a clearer belief that I am .doing what is best in the interests of my country and my Empire.
I was somewhat surprised that my hon. friend from North' Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) spent so much time, first, in proving that the voluntary system was a comparative failure, because it had not been carried on as it should have been carried on; deciding, then, that he would vote for the conscription measure on the second reading, but advising that it should be held in abeyance for some weeks or months, after which Parliament should be brought together and put it through, so that it could be satisfactorily carried out. That seems to 'be his policy. I say I am surprised that a gentleman who has such a good knowledge of world affairs should, on a question of this importance, give forth any uncertain sound. I understand tha the provincial leader of the Liberals, Mr. Rowell, recently held a meeting in his constituency, which is also that of

my hon. friend (Mr. Nesbitt)-both these gentlemen are elected by the same constituents. This meeting was held in Woodstock, and a resolution was moved by one of the gentlemen present to the effect that those present were heart and soul in favour of conscription. That resolution was carried, I understand, by a practically unanimous standing vote, and amongst those who voted, I believe, my hon. friend (Mr. Nesbitt) himself had the honour of appearing, as well as the. gentleman who was formerly representative of South Oxford and is a candidate for the next election, Mr. Schell. Having taken that stand in his own constituency, I think it was the hon. gentleman's duty to himself and the House to state more plainly his attitude and to give more whole-souled support to this measure, which is undoubtedly required, which is in the best interests of Canada and of our army at the front, as well as of the Empire as a whole.
This departure upon which the Government has embarked is the first real out-and-out war measure proposed, according to my way of thinking. It is not designed, as my hon. friend would intimate, to be a conscription of one party or another party, but of all; and I think my hon. friend is scarcely true to his own knowledge when he stated that all the matters in connection with the war have been administered with more or less of a partisan bias. I think that is not true of the county of Oxford; it certainly is not true of the neigh-' bouring county of Brant. In the county of Brant, Liberals and Conservatives have had a square deal throughout. The first man to go from Brantford in command of a contingent was a Liberal; and I can say as having had a great deal to do with the raising of the 125th Battalion, that the question of politics had nothing to do with its management or with the filling of its ranks. And I think the same conditions prevailed in Oxford.

That is what I said-
I said there was no partisanship so far as sending men. to the front was concerned.

I think that Hansard will show that I have correctly represented what the hon. gentleman, .said. He said the whole war had been conducted in a partisan way. Of course, I do not wish to misrepresent the hon. gentleman.

I said it was so reported. Mr. COCKSHUTT: Oh! But the hon. gentleman's own experience in bxford does

not warrant any such statement. My experience in Brant certainly does not warrant it; and I think that other hon. members can testify to the same effect with regard to their several counties. I say this 'is a real war measure. And I think that the Government mean business in it. If not, they certainly will not get my support for long. If they pass a Conscription Bill, declaring that they want to put it in force, and then leave it idle on the statute book and do not pugh it, I shall certainly be dissatisfied and shall criticise any turning back in this measure, or with regard to the control of food and fuel, or the grain commission.. All these are thorough war measures, the kind of measures we have been calling for for some time. My hon. friend knows that we have been calling for them, and knows that now that we have got them we expect the Government will carry them out without fear or favour. If they do not live up to my expectations, all I can say is that I do not expect to follow a Government that makes fine professions but does not carry them into effect. I believe they are honest and that they intend to carry out this law.
Then my hon. friend and I will have to form a separate party, for I quite agree with him.

I suppose I should
be very proud of one sincere follower. The hon. gentleman has told us that the voluntary system is exhausted.
No, no.

He told us that it
was not effective because it was not properly carried out.	,

No, you have a bad
memory.
I think that Hansard will show that the hon. gentleman attempted to prove that voluntary enlistment had been so bungled that we did not get the men we balled for.
No, I did not say anything of the kind.
The hon. gentleman said that officers had been put on the platform and given large money, husky chaps that ought- to be at the front.
Sure, I said that.

The voluntary system was successful to the extent of procuring for our armies over 400,000 men. I do

not think that any one is justified in describing that as a failure.
You are saying just what I said.	<

If the hon. gentleman agrees with me, I hope he will allow me to proceed. The voluntary system as carried out, I think, has been a great credit to our people. I believe that as many inen enlisted under the voluntary system in the Dominion of Canada as enlisted in any other part of the world. But it succeeded only in those parte of the country that gave it a fair trial and did their best under it. If it failed in any place, it failed because it was not pushed with sufficient vigour by the natural leaders of the people. And who are those leaders? The members of this House. The man who represents a constituency in this House is the first citizen in his riding, and he is the man who should have taken the responsibility for recruiting in that riding. There were no kid-glove methods pursued in the province of Ontario when getting recruits, let me tell my hon. friends from the province of Quebec. These hon. gentlemen tell us that the voluntary system has not had a fair chance, that it has not been pushed for all it tvas worth in Quebec as it has been in other places. Let me tell these hon. gentlemen that the same methods that were pursued in Ontario were open to them in Quebec, if they chose to employ them. How were recruits raised in the various constituencies in Ontario? The member for .the constituency-and I include the Liberals as well as Conservatives and think they deserve probably as much credit as we do; I will say that for Oxford, though I have not been closely associated with recruiting in that county; and I believe the same is true of Wellington and Lambton-put himself at the head of the movement and carried the message to all the countryside. We did not get recruits in Brant to the number of 4,000 out of a population of a little over 40,000, let me tell my hon. friend from Rou-ville (Mr. Lemieux), without putting forth exertion. The men in tne county formed themselves into a recruiting organization, including the best citizens on both sides of politics-there was no politics in it.
We did not know the politics of the men upon that recruiting committee. Men'of all parties, all races and all creeds were there. They got together, a band of citizens, believing that the life and unity of the Empire were at stake, that Christianity, civilization, liberty and religion were in the balance and, like men realizing that all these responsibilities were upon them, they placed themselves willingly in harness; their ears were at the disposal of speakers, their houses were opened to visitors who came to speak, their money was at the disposal -of the committee, and thousands and thousands of private dollars in the city of Brantford and county of Brant were spent in getting these 4,000 men together. We did not have any rosy way of doing it; it was done by solid work and I ask the hon. member from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) as he seems to be .one of the few representatives from Quebec in the Chamber now, if the same methods were fairly tried in Quebec. If they were not fairly tried in Quebec he and his fellow members should shoulder the responsibility. The responsibility rests primarily upon the members of this House from the province of Quebec if the voluntary system did not receive the support it should have received. That is gospel truth and no one can deny it. Throughout Ontario this message was carried, at every cross-roads the doctrine was preached and at every school house the flag was unfurled and the message was delivered. People who had never had much experience in speaking, who previously had been slow in speech, roused their fellow-men in a way that I had never seen equal-eld in a public meeting in the city of Brantford or the county of Brant. What was the response? From the good old province of Ontario about 180,000 voluntary recruits offered their lives on the altar of their country, and to-night many of them are laying down their lives in the trenches that you and I may enjoy our ease at home. This thing has been done and it has been done by disinterested citizens in all parts of this country. What took place in Ontario I am sure also took place throughout the whole of the West and if it has not applied to the East it is because the members, primarily of the Opposition, have not done as was done in Ontario-placed themselves at the head of a recruiting league and gone out and carried the message and planted the cross-the fiery cross-upon every road that leads to every town, city, and hamlet in Quebec. I feel confident if that had been done the response from Quebec would have been better than it has been.
We are told that this is a fit subject io^ * a referendum. Governments in this country have not frequently shifted their responsibility and placed upon the people the lead that they themselves should take. That

has not been the vogue in Canada. It may be wrong. In Australia they pursue a different course but in this country Governments have shouldered the responsibility with regard to all the questions they have had tp deal with and they have placed them, fairly and squarely before the people. But now we have the policy proposed of a referendum to the people so as to allow the slacker, the man who has not gone under the voluntary system, to say that he will not go under the compulsory system; while our 400,000 soldiers are out of the country. Is that a fair proposition? No.
This is not a fit subject for a referendum because in many cases the voter to whom it will be submitted is not a fair and impartially-minded man to give a decision on such a subject. If the liberties are worth having they are worth fighting for, and if the liberties which we in Canada enj.oy are as great as we think they are, they are worthy of the best efforts of every citizen.
I do not want to reprove my fellow citizens from Quebec. I am sorry to disagree with them on a question of such great importance, but I must say that Quebec has been the greatest disappointment to me in the whole war. I say that from the bottom of my heart. When this war began I thought: Now, Canada will be a united country; never have we been entirely united but now we will be absolutely united. Look at the great, old land of France, valorous, brilliant France; there she is with every man available, every woman, every child throwing their lives into 1 he struggle spending their last ounce of energy, their last drop of bipod, in defence of the great old land that gave our friends their language and their liberties in the first place, and to whom they owe a great deal of. what they possess. I said: There will be no doubt about the position of Quebec on this great question, because all her people will stand shoulder to shoulder with us. But now is there to be a referendum-to all the people of Canada?-No; to the people who stay at home, to the people who should have gone but who did not go. It has remained for the province ,of Quebec to furnish, in my mind, the most pathetic and outstanding figure in Canada in this whole war.
I am sorry that the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier) is not here because I wanted to make a Special appeal to him. I was going to propose one referendum that he should make. Although I disapprove pf the spirit of the proposal I would g ve in.to the extent of such a referendum as that which I pro-

pose. I would be willing and delighted to pay the expenses of this particular referendum if my right hpn. friend would make it. What is it? It is that he immediately send a wireless message to Dr. Beland, the exPostmaster General in his own Government, telling him the situation in which we are placed in Canada to-day in regard to recruiting and conscription and asking him, on behalf of his own people here, tp tell them truly what in his heart he thinks should be done. If such a message were sent to Dr. Beland, I can imagine that a reply would come back, written almost with his life blood, that must appeal to every Quebec citizen: Recall your resolution, recant your opinions, repent of your mistake and come; stay not upon the order of your coming, but come. Let me appeal tq the pity of my hon. friends from Quebec-Dr. Beland, visiting in the neutral country of Belgium, seized upon almost immediately after war broke out; his new bride done to death by the ruthless Hun; he, himself while we are here debating and discussing ways and means, eating the bread and drinking the water of affliction in Germany, a man who cannot move hand or foot with out the permission of the Huns! Is this a time to sit here in idle debate? Is this a time to say that you cannot dp any more than you have done? No, Sir, let that referendum be taken and if my friend does not answer somewhat in the line I have indicated, then I think I might almost venture to oppose the Bill myself.

about it, but I do not think the people of Quebec can escape defending our common country, because we do not speak as good French in Ontario as we should.
I have spoken strongly on this .question, and I feel strongly. It is a profound regret to me, personally, that I have not the support of my hon. friends on the other side of the House, especially the members from Quebec. I feel that they have misjudged the situation, and are not prizing the liberties that have been theirs under the British flag and Crown. I ask them to

repent, ere it is too late, and join us, and, in one united effort, let us "bring the war to a close, because if we allow the enemy to defeat us in this matter, we will only regret it once, and that will be for all time to come.
An attempt has been made, on the part of many, to confuse the one issue in this Bill, and we hear a great- deal about the consoription of wealth. The hon. gentleman from South Renfrew dwelt on that at great length, and the Finance Minister has replied very ably. I look upon this and other matters which have been discussed as side issues, which have nothing to do with the question before the House. These questions have been dragged in, but are not properly matters to be discussed in this debate. The conscription of wealth is a subject by itself, which seems to be not very well defined, and the Finance Minister tells us he has been able so far and expects to be able, in the future, to furnish all the funds that are required for the war. We want the men, and the money will take care of itself, and will be provided in due course. The ministers of every denomination have preached conscription of wealth as well as of men. I attended a church meeting this week, and this question came up, and in my own church I said what I am not afraid to say here, that this proposition, with regard to the conscription of wealth, is going to hit some of the preachers, if it is carried, and I think it started them puzzling a little bit. Let it be remembered that, if you conscript a man, you take the whole of him, and do not leave a leg or arm behind, and you require a good sound man. If the conscription of wealth means the same thing it is going to take the whole pile of wealth which a man possesses, leaving nothing. Many of our clergymen brethren are lords over a great pile of money. I think Quebec can tell us something about that as well as Ontario. It must be remembered that, if conscription of wealth is coming, some of the churches are going to be hit. It reminds me of a remark a Six Nation Indian used to make, when they told him the preacher had given them a very poor ser-mon-" Well, it was poor pay and poor preach. It will Ibe a good deal the same with our clerical brethren. If all the wealth be conscripted the churches will not be supported as they have been. Wealth has been accumulated by many of the religious bodies, and the clerical gentleman cannot refuse to obey the scriptural teaching, that a man should always pay taxes
and obligations of that kind, especially if he is a religious man. I throw out that flint to the preachers who are propounding this doctrine from the pulpit: that the conscription of wealth will take the accumulated wealth of the churches, as well as the wealth of the individuals. We are all prepared for that to the tull extent necessary to conduct this war to a finish. Canada has the right to expect from its citizens the surrender of all -that they possess to be used in defence of the country. In other words, the rights of the State are superior to the rights of any individuals. That is a strong doctrine perhaps to preach, but it will be found to be absolutely true. It has been the price of liberty and freedom for all time, and always will be. The state; which is the accumulation and union of individuals is always superior to the units which compose the whole. The State at the present time says we want men, we want more men, they have not volunteered. We are bringing down legislation to conscript these men, or, to use a selective draft, or whatever you wish, and put them into line. These men will be selected without fear or favour by the powers that be.
It has been stated in the House on several occasions that our soldiers are not paid as they should be paid, and that we are making them serve for a very much less wage than they could earn in any of the ordinary walks of life. While that may be the case, can any gentleman present tell me of any soldier in the world who is better paid than the Canadian. I have yet to hear of him. Therefore, I do not think we can be accused of being niggardly. What was the pay of the French soldier when the war broke out? A penny a day, raised since, I believe, to five cents. The German pay is so small you do not hear of it at all. The British pay is less than half of ours, and the Australian pay is less than ours. Being in constant communication with those at the front, having blood relations there, I think I know what I am speaking about when I say that the Canadian soldier is one of the best treated men and one of the best soldiers the world has ever seen. The pay never was presumed to compensate him for his effort. The soldier's life is presumed to be sacrificed to the State. No money value can be placed on that life. It is beyond price, and cannot be measured by dollars and cents. It is a gift from God. A man who goes to the trenches, and lays his life on the altar of his country, cannot be paid in money. People have raised the bogey



that the pay of the Canadian soldier is insufficient, but the pay never induces these men to join the ranks. The first contingent did not enlist because the men desired to draw $1.10 a day, nor did any of the subsequent contingents go to the front on account of the remuneration. They said: our country needs us at the front; by Divine Providence I have been created a man fit to serve; I am sound in wind and limb;
I place my services on the altar of my country, and the $1.10 or $2, or $5 per day I get amounts to nothing;
I am fighting because I believe in the cause. I am fighting because my King and country need me; I am fighting for the liberties of my people, and in order that the British race may be supreme in the future as it has been in the past; these are the things that have appealed to me- not the paltry $1.10 a day. Mr. Speaker, you cannot pay these men with money; it is folly to try to raise the bogey of our men being insufficiently paid and of that being the reason for lack of enlistment. In most instances, our men are getting all the pay that they expected, and all that they asked. But they do want to be sustained in their work; they ask that we at home, instead of bickering and quarrelling over minor matters of detail, should get together and, in conjunction with the boys overseas, present a united front to the Hun and give him to understand that we are in the fight to a finish. I do not like the clause of this Bill-it happens to be No. 13, the unlucky number-which limits the number of men required to 100,000. We may need more men than that. We must give all that the successful prosecution of the war requires; we have engaged to do our part to the utmost of our ability and to the limit of our resources. Therefore I say that this section of the Bill should be struck out.
It has been said that labour is opposed to conscription. Well, I come from a town in which 7,000 of the citizens work in factories and earn their, daily bread at the bench. While a handful of them, in meeting assembled, did pass a resolution against conscription some weeks ago, I do not think that their opinion represents the attitude of labour. I do not believe that the views of the gentlemen who met in Ottawa represent the attitude of labour. I believe that the attitude of labour now is what it has been; the testimony of the men in the trenches is the best answer to the assertion that labour is opposed to conscription. From 100,000 to 150,000 workingmen are either 
fighting in the trenches or are ready to go to the front when they are needed. It is plainly evident that this war is a war of the people. Every class is in line to do its part in the prosecution of the war-from the richest to the poorest, from the highest to the lowest. To say that the wealthy man has not done anything because his wealth has not been conscripted is simply begging the question. I do not know that there are any millionaires in the community from which1 I come, but I believe that the sons of the well-to-do in the county of Brant have gone to the front in just as great numbers as the sons of the needy and the poor. The comradeship and the good feeling that has prevailed among the men and the officers who have gone to the front has done my heart good on many occasions. I know of university boys from Brantford, qualified lawyers and medical men, who have enlisted in the ranks. One young man in particular was offered a commission. He said:	No, I am no soldier; I know my
limitations; I know that without experience I am not fit to lead men; I will go and fight my way upwards from the ranks. That boy came from one of the best families in Brantford; he had been accustomed to the very best living that the city could furnish. He went overseas and put in a year and a half in the trenches as a private. He qualified for a lieutenant's commission, and a month afterwards fell while leading the platoon that my own son had been leading. His body has not been recovered and his friends do not know where that body lies. I mention that only to show the spirit that prevails among the men. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that if we in this House had applied ourselves as diligently to carrying out the requirements of the war as we have to finding fault with each other, things would be very different from what they are today. This war is far /rom being over. The submarines are taking a very heavy toll of the mercantile marine; this week 27 or 28 of the largest British ships of the line have been sunk. The men at the front need help; the situation is serious. I believe that the House should put this measure through as quickly as possible and that both sides of the House should get behind it and make it successful. We should present a united front in obtaining the 100,000 men, or whatever number is required, drilling them, equipping them and getting them to the firing line, thus saving many lives and perhaps, materially shortening the war. It

260ft
is up to Canada to do as she ha* done in the past. She has done nobly, but let her not now spoil her splendid record of three years by faltering or giving evidences of decay. Let her be just as resolute, just as firm as she was in August, 1914. Let us now be just as firmly resolved as we were at that time to carry the grand old flag to victory; to ensure the freedom and the liberty of the nations of Europe, both small and great. 1 have had occasion to criticise the great nation to the south of us; I have even been termed an anti-American. But I rejoice now that the people of the United States ai\e shoulder to shoulder with us in the great fight for the liberty of the world. Only last January I criticised President Wilson; I thought that he deserved criticism. I want to withdraw that criticism now in same degree and give him credit for having thrown himself into the war as few statesmen on either side of the Atlantic have done. Every step that he has taken has been wisely conceived. In the United States they are giving the very best that they can of their wealth and of their energy to the prosecution of the war. They are forming aviation corps; sending ships across the sea and building more; taking other steps to help the' Allies. That, Mr. Speaker, should give us encouragement. That should cause us to resolve anew that we will continue the great work we have undertaken. I believe that, by the providence of God, the British Empire and its Allies-France, Italy, Russia, Belgium, Serbia, Roumania, Japan and the United States -will secure a vindication of the principles of liberty and justice which they have enunciated and will be justified in their upholding of the right of smaller nations to live in peace and amity and to have absolute control of their own affairs.
Although history may contain pages that contain more words and tales that take longer to tell, history will contain no prouder or brighter page than that which tells of the noble part that has been played by the Dominion of Canada up to the present time on the battlefields of Europe, and if we at home are only as good, true, and honest in our hearts as the men whom we have sent to the front, we shall have no regrets; we shall have nothing to recall; but we shall have the proud satisfaction of a good heart and a clear conscience in the presence of both God and man.

Mr. Speaker, it is my intention to confine
166J
my remarks almost wholly to the measure before the House, and to give this House my reasons why it is my intention to support that measure. I am going to make my position clear at the commencement of my remarks. We are in a serious stage of the history of Canada; not only have we before us the winning of the war, but those of us who look at questions from a national standpoint are fearful for national unity, and in my remarks to-night I do not wish to say anything that will be a .reflection upon any other province or section of the Dominion of Canada. I do not feel that I have any right to cast any reflection of that kind. I feel that if some of us, coming from other provinces of this country, had to face the conditions that have been faced in the province that has been frequently mentioned in this debate we would not be so boastful of our position in this war. No poison has been spread abroad in our provinces. If that poison had been spread abroad there might have been a different attitude on the part of many people in the other provinces at this particular period in our history.
I am in favour of conscription because I believe that this is Canada's war; that we are fighting for our own defence and for our own existence. That is why I have said, on many occasions since this war commenced, that we must give the last man and the last dollar to win it. Why do I say that? I do not want to boast that I can make my position clear to the people of other provinces that do not see as I do, but I believe that all fair-minded . people throughout this country could be convinced that this war is actually Canada's war. If, after the war commenced, Great Britain had not gone into this [DOT]struggle in Europe, and if we had not entered it, and if as a result of the war between Germany on the one hand and Russia and France on the other, Russia and France had been conquered, Germany would have been dominant in Europe, and Great Britain and the'British Empire and the United States would have been in danger whether they went into the war or not. We may have to resort to conscription now, but under those circumstances we would have had to have larger armed forces; we would have had to spend more money in the maintenance of troops than we have ever had to do in our history, because we would have had to protect ourselves against the dominant power of the world. When Gieat Britain went into this war we were part of the British Empire,
One can apply for another or for a number of others.

If that is the case I am perfectly satisfied, but I want to make it clear that instances of that kind might occur; I know they would occur in my own part of the country. Many men would
not ask for exemption, afid the board might not know the men's circumstances.
There is another matter that I should like to emphasize, and that is this. In all the communications I have had from my part of the country since the Bill was introduced and its contents made known, there is the feeling that it should be brought into effect without much delay. Now I am in agreement with those who urge that if possible we should give another chance to voluntary recruiting, but if we are not going to do that, if the need is as great as we are told it is, there should be no hesitation in bringing the Bill into effect.
There is another matter. In the provinces of the West at any rate, where the sentiment is absolutely sounu behind this war, no man would be exempted by the boards that would 'be constituted in that part of the country unless he was absolutely entitled to exemption There is a possibility that in other parts of the country the sentiment of the boards would not foe of that character and that men would be exempted who had no right to be exempted. There is the right to appeal under the Bill, 'but that involves delay. In the provinces of the West we have already fulfilled our obligations and raised more than our quota. With the sentiment of the boards out there behind the Act it might p.ossibly be that from those provinces alone almost the whole of the 100,000 men required under the Act would foe raised; there is that possibility; I do not say it would occur. This is certain, however: no slacker in Western Canada who is not required in that country in pursuits that are necessary for the successful prosecution of the war will be exempted by any of the boards appointed, unless the board should be dominated by men who would display favouritism to individuals, and I hope that will not be the case.
As to the amendment moved by my right hon. leader, I might say as a personal matter that I was not born into the Liberal doctrine. I did not inherit my Liberalism, but became possessed of it because of my high regard of Sir Wilfrid Laurier back in the days when I first commenced to take an interest in public affairs. I love and respect him, always have, and always hope to do so. He has been an ideal to. me in many respects, but in this particular matter I honestly differ with him. I believe the view he has taken to be an absolutely honest view, and that he thinks it is in the best interests of unity and the welfare of the

country. But I do not think the referendum would reach the object I have in view. I believie that conscription is necessary. I believe I am a member of this House at a critical time in the history of Canada and in tlie history of the world. I have a duty to perform, and I am prepared to perform it by declaring myself absolutely in favour of conscription. I am prepared to face my people on the stand I have taken, and to accept the consequences whatever they may be.
I do not want the men who, I feel, are neglecting their duty at this time, to have an opportunity of saying whether they should stay at home or not. I want to see these men go forward and serve their country. They have refused to go under a voluntary system, and they must go under some other system. And if these men go forward under a system of conscription, go to the front and perform their duty, they will come back to Canada, I believe, thankful to this Parliament that they were sent forward, even under compulsion, because they will feel in after years proud of the fact that they participated in this war, and we hope they will participate in it to save liberty, justice, and democracy and to prevent the domination of this world by the Germans.
I have very strong views on another matter which has been frequently mentioned in this debate, one that I have mentioned on other occasions during the present session. I will not use, in describing if, the term that is quite often used, because I think that 'term does not set forth its real meaning. I refer to taxation. We must have taxation that will make the people realize that we are undergoing a real strain on account of this war. My hon. friend, the president of the Patriotic Fund (Sir Herbert Ames) had a slogan, " Give until it hurts." I suggest that the Minister of Finance should tax the people until it hurts.. We cannot expect to have conscription carried into effect and our young men who are sent to the front go forward satisfied unless they feel that those who are left at home also are bearing a heavy burden. This is not the case at the present time. I know in my own city men who are not being reached in any exceptional way by taxation, men of wealth who are not being forced to pay one red cent ,nto the treasury of this country except through the tariff. These men also are neglecting their duty; they are financial shirkers. And if we are dealing with the men who are shirking their duty .for service overseas why not deal also with the men
[Mr. Buchanan.l
who are shirking their duties at home? The income tax has been mentioned. I have a letter to-day from a very prominent citizen of Lethbridge giving his views on conscription. He declares himself in favour of conscription, but says, also, that he 'Was in favour of the conscription of wealth-he uses those words. He intimates that, though he has an income of about $10,006 a year, he was not being reached in any way. He says that he and such as he ought to be reached, that there ought to be some form of taxation that will make them realize that the war is taking place and that they have to do their duty as much as the men who are forced to go overseas to defend the country. This gentleman is a liberal contributor to the Patriotic Fund, the Red Cross, and other good movements; he is one to whom we can go at any time and get a generous contribution for a good cause. Still, he feels that he is not doing his duty and that he ought to be taxed. The Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) told us this afternoon that financially everything was all right. But we must remember that when this war is over financially things may be all wrong. Now is the time to get at the people. They are prosperous; they are making money, many of them making money out of the prosperity due to this war. We should not hesitate to impose income taxes upon our people, and heavy income taxes. I could mention case after case that strengthens my opinion in favour of a tax of this nature. We do not want any favouritism in our war policy; everybody should be forced to make sacrifices at some time or other. There are many men of wealth who are not doing their part in this war. While many are giving handsomely to the Red Cross and the Patriotic Fund, everybody is not doing so. Many are not doing anything to maintain our position in this war If they will not do their duty voluntarily, then let us force these shirkers to come through with good contributions directly to the public treasury.
In closing, I wish to give expression to what I believe to be our duty at this time. I think it is our duty to establish in this country a government representative of all classes and all occupations-at least the occupations necessary to the prosecution of the war. In saying this, I make no reflections upon the Government or any member of it. In speaking as I do I wish to make reference to labour and agriculture especially. I quite appreciate the attitude that the labour men take in this matter of conscription. In my own city, the labour

men are demanding what is called the conscription of wealth. They are quite satisfied to have conscription of manhood if there is conscription of wealth. But there are the same feelings between employers and employees as in times of peace. They want to see the man with money doing his part. If we had a Government at this time, whether partisan, or coalition, or National, with a read representative of labour, as one of its members, a man who had the confidence of labour from the Atlantic to the Pacific, I think we should avoid, for instance, strikes in the coal mines of western Canada; I think we should get the labouring men behind conscription and every other war measure.
Again, with regard to agriculture, there is talk, for instance, of fixing the price of wheat, and other measures affecting the farm. All this could be best done by having in the Government a real representative of the farmers, a man who could go to the farmers and have such influence with them that he could get them to do what is necessary. There are men of that kind, I know, in western Canada-big men, men of influence and ability, men thoroughly in earnest about this war. In all honesty, we cannot have a successful prosecution of the war until we have in existence in this country a government that has the confidence, not of one party only, but of the whole people. That is the request I make to-night-that we constitute in this country, for the period of the war at any rate, a government that shall have the confidence of the people, that will prosecute the war to a successful issue, a government that will not be for party but will be for the state entirely and all the time. If we have a government of that kind from now on until the conclusion of the war, many of the problems that face us will be- solved; much of discord that exists will pass away.
I think I have made my position clear. I am in favour of conscription because I think it is the only possible method we now have left of providing reinforcements for our men at the front. I will support the measure and I wiill appear before my people and defend my course. I am satisfied that, from their record since the commencement of the present war to the present, they will endorse .the. attitude which I take with the view of doing everything possible to assist in carrying on this war to a successful conclusion.
